if a son of good family...
If a virtuous woman who studies and recites the Prajñāpāramitā should encounter those wishing to harm her, they will naturally perish, repelled by the majestic spiritual power of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said:
"Should there be those who plot against it, wherever they come from, they shall fight right there; their destruction shall be such that they can never succeed again.
The Four Heavenly Kings will all provide protection."

If these sons or daughters of good family enter into the Prajñāpāramitā and contemplate it, they will act with sovereign mastery; their speech will be like nectar, their words will be entirely honored, anger will not arise, and they will not be conceited.

The Four Heavenly Kings shall all provide protection for these good men and good women who study, uphold, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā. Whatever they say will not be otherwise; their words will be like nectar, their speech will not be disparaging, anger will not arise, and self-conceit will not be produced.
Why is this? Because they practice the Prajñāpāramitā.
They do not cherish arrogance, they do not cherish self-will, and they do not cherish anger.
These good sons and good daughters will naturally give rise to this thought in their minds:
"If there is conflict or strife, one should always remain far removed from it.
They will feel personal shame and reflect:
"These people are so evil that they are not to be approached.
He thought to himself:
"I seek the Way of the Buddha; I must not follow words of anger and hatred, but must quickly cause myself to attain a state of good heart."
Whatever these sons and daughters of good family have performed, they shall all see for themselves as present merit; it is the same for those who study, uphold, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is difficult to fathom, O God among Gods!
One who practices the Prajñāpāramitā transcends all evils and acts with sovereign mastery; there is no one equal to them."
The Buddha said to Śakra-devānām-indra:

"Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family studies, upholds, and recites the Prajñāpāramitā, they shall never fear even when passing through the midst of extreme perils; even if they enter an army, they shall not be struck by weapons."
The Buddha said:
"What I have spoken is without exception.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family recites the Prajñāpāramitā at that time, even if they were to die therein, or if enemies therein should wish to harm them, it will be exactly as I have spoken—without exception—and these sons and daughters of good family shall never meet with an untimely death therein."
Even if one were in their midst, should there be an archer or someone with weapons directed at them, they would never strike their body. Why is this?
This Prajñāpāramitā is the supreme great mantra, the honored mantra.

Those who study this mantra—whether they be good men or good women—will not think of evil for themselves, nor will they think of evil toward others; being entirely free from thoughts of evil, they shall become heroes among men, attain Buddhahood for themselves, and protect all people.
Those who study this spell will swiftly attain Buddhahood.

Furthermore, Kauśika, if one writes down the Prajñāpāramitā and studies, maintains, and recites it, neither humans nor non-humans shall be able to harm them, except for the consequences of offenses committed in past lives which cannot be avoided by request.
If one enters the place where the Buddha first attained the Way from whichever direction they may come, no ghosts, spirits, birds, or beasts that wish to cause harm will ever be able to injure them.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have each attained Buddhahood from this very place.
For this reason, he is not afraid, not terrified, and has no fear or dread.
"The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: wherever it resides, everyone shall pay homage to it, revere it, and protect it.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there is such a thing, O God among Gods!"

If one writes out the *Prajñāpāramitā*, upholds the sutra scrolls, takes refuge in them, pays homage, and serves them; or if one offers to them named flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, silken fabrics, flower canopies, banners, and streamers; and if there is another who, having taken the relics of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, erects a stupa for them, takes refuge in them, pays homage, and serves them; and offers to them fine flowers, renowned incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, silken fabrics, flower canopies, banners, and streamers to make offerings—[the merit of the latter is greater].
The Buddha asked Kauśika:
"In this way, which of these merits would be greater?
It depends on the retribution one desires."
"What do you think, Kauśika!

How did the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having attained sarvajñatā himself, manifest the body of a Buddha, and by training in which dharma did he attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and become a perfectly awakened one?"
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"The Tathāgata studied the Prajñāpāramitā and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, thereby personally achieving the state of an Arhat-samyak-saṃbuddha."
The Buddha said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
"It is not for the sake of bodily relics that one becomes a Buddha;
rather, it is from sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) that one attains Buddhahood. A Tathāgata emerges from the Prajñāpāramitā."
Thus it is, Kauśika!
The body of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) emerges from the prajñāpāramitā;
the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is born from sarvajñatā.
When I have attained the body of a Buddha, after my parinirvāṇa, my relics shall also receive offerings.

If there are good men or good women who write down the Prajñāpāramitā, study, uphold, recite, and practice it; who take refuge in it, pay homage, and serve it; and who offer it fine flowers, renowned incense, powdered incense, blended incense, fragrant oils, burning incense, silken banners, canopies, and pennants—this constitutes making an offering to the wisdom of sarvajña (omniscience).
Furthermore, Kauśika!

If there are those who write down the Prajñāpāramitā, and though they do not read the scroll, they merely make offerings to it and pay homage to it, these good men and good women will obtain incomparable merit from this.
"Why is this? It is for the sake of making offerings to the wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, O God among Gods!
Those people of Jambudvīpa who do not make offerings to and serve the *prajñāpāramitā* are those who do not know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is supreme; they shall obtain incomparable merit."
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"How is it, Kauśika!
Among the people of Jambudvīpa, how many are there who have faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus?"
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The people of Jambudvīpa are few; those who believe in the Buddha, believe in the Dharma, and believe in the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus are but very few indeed.”
Furthermore, those who practice as stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, or pratyekabuddhas are very few;
those who are able to proceed toward the path of the Buddha-way are likewise very few indeed.
The Buddha said, “It is so,
Kauśika! Those who seek to practice the path to Buddhahood are likewise very few indeed.”

There are incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* numbers of people who seek Buddhahood and wish to practice the bodhisattva path; yet, among them, only one or two emerge and establish themselves on the stage of *avaivartika*.
For this reason, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family who practices seeking the Buddha-way studies, upholds, and recites the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, they should pay homage, serve, and revere them.
Why is this? It is because they have mastered the Prajñāpāramitā.
All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past originally learned it by practicing the Prajñāpāramitā as Bodhisattvas; I, too, at that time, studied within it.
After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas shall all receive this Prajñāpāramitā.
After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take up relics for veneration, erect stupas made of the seven precious substances, and throughout their entire lives take refuge in them, pay homage, serve, and make offerings—offering celestial flowers, powdered incense, unguent incense, burning incense, blended incenses, celestial silken banners, canopies, standards, and pennants—what do you think, Kauśika, would the merit resulting from such actions be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"Very much, very much,
O Heaven among Heavens!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious as for a son or daughter of good family to write out the Prajñāpāramitā, to take up the scroll, to take refuge in it, to pay homage and serve it, and to make offerings of famous flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and pennants; the merit obtained is exceedingly great."
The Buddha said:
"Set aside this stūpa, Kausika!

If there were stupas filled with the seven treasures throughout Jambudvīpa, and a son or daughter of good family, for as long as they live, took refuge in them, paid homage, and served them, making offerings of celestial flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, fragrant unguents, burning incense, celestial silks, flowered canopies, banners, and streamers.
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious for a son or daughter of good family to write out the Prajñāpāramitā, to take up the scroll, to take refuge in it, to pay homage, and to serve it by making offerings of famous incense, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags, than for them to obtain such exceedingly great merit."
The Buddha said:
"Set aside for a moment the stūpas built in this Jambudvīpa.
Suppose, Kauśika, there were stūpas made of the seven treasures filling the four continents!"

If good sons or good daughters, for as long as they live, take refuge, pay homage, and serve [the Buddha], making offerings of celestial flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, celestial silks, flower canopies, banners, and streamers.
"Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied,
"It would be very great, very great!"
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious for a son of good family or a daughter of good family to merely [worship] as it is for them to write out the Prajñāpāramitā, take up the scroll, take refuge in it, pay homage, and serve it, making offerings of famous flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, fragrant oils, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags; thus they shall obtain far more merit."
The Buddha said:
"Setting aside the stupas for the four continents, Kausika!

Suppose there were a single world-system, and furthermore another world-system, and likewise a thousand such world-systems, all four sides of which were filled with stupas made of the seven treasures.

If a son or daughter of good family, for as long as they live, took refuge in them, paid homage, served them, and made offerings of celestial flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incenses, unguents, burning incense, celestial silks, flowered canopies, banners, and pennants; [the merit would be immeasurable].
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"Very much, very much,
O God among Gods!
the Buddha said.

"It is not as meritorious for a good man or a good woman to write out the Prajñāpāramitā, to take up the scroll, to take refuge in it, to pay homage and serve it, and to offer it with famous flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, fragrant oils, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, and streamers; the merit obtained from these is far greater."
The Buddha said:
"Setting aside a thousand worlds, Kauśika!
Furthermore, consider a thousand minor kingdoms; within these two thousand kingdoms, every side is filled with stūpas made of the seven treasures."

If good sons or good daughters, for as long as they live, take refuge, pay homage, and serve [the Buddha], making offerings of celestial flowers, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, celestial silks, canopies, banners, and streamers.
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much, very much,
O God among Gods!
the Buddha said.

"It is not as meritorious for a son or daughter of good family to write down the Prajñāpāramitā, to uphold the sutra, to take refuge in it, to pay homage and serve it, and to offer it fine flowers, excellent incense, powdered incense, blended incense, fragrant oils, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, and streamers, as the merit they thereby obtain is exceedingly great."
The Buddha said,
"Set aside the lands of two thousand central kingdoms, Kauśika!

Suppose there were seven-jeweled stupas filling the four directions of a trichiliocosm; if there were sons or daughters of good family who, for as long as they lived, took refuge in them, paid homage, served them, and made offerings of celestial flowers, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, celestial silks, canopies, banners, and streamers.
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"Very much, very much,
O God among Gods!
the Buddha said.

"It is not as meritorious for a son or daughter of good family to write out the Prajñāpāramitā, to take up the scroll, to take refuge in it, to pay homage and serve it, and to offer it fine flowers, excellent incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags, than for them to obtain such vast merit."
The Buddha said:
"Set aside, Kauśika, the seven-jeweled stūpas filling a trichiliocosm."

If all the bodhisattvas within the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were to become human beings, and each person were to construct a stupa made of the seven treasures, and these people were to offer worship throughout their entire lives with music, song, and dance; with various celestial incenses, famous flowers, powdered incense, liquid perfumes, and burning incense; and with silken banners, canopies, and pennants.
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Is the merit and virtue of this not great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“The merit and virtue of what they have performed is exceedingly great, exceedingly great,
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It would not be as meritorious for a son or daughter of good family to write out the Prajñāpāramitā, to take up its scrolls, to take refuge in them, to pay homage and serve them, and to offer them famous flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and victory standards, than for them to obtain far more merit [by the former act]."
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is, so it is!
O God among Gods!”
Those who take refuge in the Prajñāpāramitā, pay homage to it, and serve it, have thereby already made offerings to the omniscience (sarvajñatā) of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Śakra Devānām-indra again addressed the Buddha:
"Setting aside the people of the trichiliocosm, each of whom has erected a stūpa made of the seven precious substances;

suppose that as many people as fill Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were each to erect stūpas made of the seven precious substances, and they were all to make offerings for one kalpa and even another kalpa, using celestial flowers, famous incenses, powdered incense, blended incense, fragrant ointments, burning incense, celestial silks, flowered canopies, banners, and streamers, and employing all the various musical performances of the heavens above and below to make these offerings."

The merit and virtue of that [person] is not equal to that of a son of good family or a daughter of good family who writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, takes up the scroll, takes refuge in it, pays homage, and serves it, making offerings of famous flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags.
"The merit obtained from all [other sources] is surpassed by that.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"It is so, Kauśika!"

It is not equal to the merit obtained by a son of good family or a daughter of good family from within the Dharma, which is infinitely great—incalculable, inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and unsurpassed.
Why is this? Kauśika!
The sarvajñā (all-knowledge) of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha arises from the Prajñāpāramitā.
Thus it is, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, takes up its scrolls, takes refuge in them, pays homage, and serves them, making offerings of famous flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, silken fabrics, flower canopies, banners, and pennants.
"Thus it is, Kauśika!
All of this is brought about by the merit of their previous lives.
The Buddha said:

"Even if one were to erect stupas made of the seven treasures throughout as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand along the Ganges River—hundredfold, they would not even enter into calculation; thousandfold, they would not enter into calculation; hundred-thousandfold, they would not enter into calculation; ten-thousand-billionfold, they would not enter into calculation; and countless times over, they would still not enter into the calculation of making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā."
At that time, the forty thousand devaputras who had come to the assembly together with Śakra all said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
"Venerable One, you should take up the Prajñāpāramitā!"
"One should recite the Prajñāpāramitā!
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra,
"One should study, uphold, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā."
For what reason?
If an asura conceives the thought of raising an army to wage war against the Trāyastriṃśa devas,
at that time, Kauśika!
"When one recites the Prajñāpāramitā,
the asuras will immediately cease their hostilities, and the multitude will return.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is the supreme great mantra.
O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the most honored mantra, the peerless mantra.”
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Kauśika!"
The Prajñāpāramitā is the supreme great mantra; the Prajñāpāramitā is the most honored mantra; the Prajñāpāramitā is the peerless mantra.

Kou-yi, as for this mantra, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past attained Buddhahood by means of this very mantra; all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who are yet to come shall likewise study this mantra and attain Buddhahood; and all the Buddhas of the present also attain Buddhahood by means of this very mantra.

O Kauśika! This spell brings forth the merit of the ten wholesome paths of action to illuminate the world, and it illuminates the world with the four dhyānas, the four truths, the four bases of psychic power, and the five supernormal powers.
By means of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to the merit of the ten wholesome paths of action,
which illuminates the world. Furthermore, Kauśika,
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family studies, maintains, and recites the *prajñāpāramitā*, they shall immediately attain the hearing of the Dharma in the present life.
Śakra Devānām Indra asked the Buddha,
“How should one listen to the Dharma of the present?
The Buddha said:
"That person shall never die an untimely death; they shall never die by poison; they shall never die by drowning; they shall never die by the blade.

Even if at times they encounter government officials or are oppressed by government officials, they should recite and contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā; when they go before them, those officials shall ultimately be unable to cause them harm."
Why is this? Because they are protected by the Prajñāpāramitā.
If one is summoned by government officials, one should recite and contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā.
If, in that place, he should meet with a king, a crown prince, or a high minister sent by them, they will immediately exchange pleasant words and all will rejoice. Why is this?
Because of his study of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Because he possesses a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, pitying and cherishing all people, down to the smallest insects that fly and crawl,
those who wish to harm him cannot find an opportunity.
When the Buddha spoke these words, a certain heterodox practitioner saw the Buddha from afar and intended to go and disturb his assembly.
Śakra Devānām-indra thought to himself:
"May I always remain by the Buddha's side for the remainder of my life to receive and recite the Prajñāpāramitā.
Should those followers of heterodox paths come here, they will surely disturb me and prevent me from receiving the Prajñāpāramitā."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, received [the teaching] from the Buddha and recited the Prajñāpāramitā.
Those heterodox practitioners, from a great distance, circumambulated the God among Gods once and then departed by way of their own path.
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"How is it that these followers of other paths have departed from among them midway?
The Buddha, knowing what Śāriputra was thinking, immediately said:
"These heterodox practitioners have no good intentions in coming here.
Śakra-devānām-indra has been contemplating the *prajñāpāramitā*, and for that reason he has turned back midway.
Thus did Māra, the Evil One, think.

“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha sits together with his fourfold assembly of disciples; the gods of the desire realm, the Brahmā gods, and all the sons of heaven are likewise present therein without exception. Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who now receive their prediction shall become leaders among men and will themselves attain Buddhahood.”
"I shall go and disturb him.
Māra, the Wicked One, transformed himself into one who rode a single-axle chariot yoked to four horses, and gradually approached the place where the Buddha was.
Śakra-devānām-indra thought to himself:
“The Wicked Māra is riding a chariot drawn by four horses, intending to come to where the Buddha is.

This is not King Bimbisāra’s chariot drawn by four horses, nor is it similar to King Prasenajit’s chariot drawn by four horses, nor is it like the chariots drawn by four horses belonging to the Śākya or the Koliya clans.”
This is inconsistent; it is the work of the degenerate Māra.
He constantly seeks an opportunity against the Buddha, wishing to disturb the people of the world.
Śakra-devānām-indra constantly aspires to recite and read the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that moment, as he focused his mind on the Prajñāpāramitā, desiring to reach its ultimate realization, Māra immediately turned back and departed.
The inhabitants of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven took the transformed flowers and, flying through the air, scattered them over the Buddha.
They all said,
"May the Prajñāpāramitā remain long in Jambudvīpa, so that all people may hear and see it. Having spoken thus,
they took various kinds of celestial flowers and scattered them over the Buddha.
They all said:
"Those who practice the Prajñāpāramitā and those who maintain the Prajñāpāramitā will not be given any opportunity for harm by Māra or the gods of Māra."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Those who hear this Prajñāpāramitā possess no small amount of merit and virtue; how much more so for those who study, recite, and uphold it, and having studied and recited it, further teach it to others? Such persons must have already seen the Buddhas in previous lives and heard the Prajñāpāramitā from them."
How much more so for one who, having studied and maintained the recitation, acts according to the matters therein; such a person has already made an offering to the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Those who wish to attain sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) must proceed from the Prajñāpāramitā.
Just as one who wishes to obtain the most supreme celestial jewels, O God among Gods,
must go to the great ocean; so too,
O God among Gods, one who wishes to obtain the precious jewel of *sarvajñatā* [all-knowledge] must likewise proceed.
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha should be sought from the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is!”
"Kauśika! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha emerges from sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"There is no one who speaks of the dānapāramitā, nor of the śīlapāramitā, nor of the kṣāntipāramitā, nor of the vīryapāramitā, nor of the dhyānapāramitā; there is absolutely no mention of these names, but only the Prajñāpāramitā is spoken of together."
"For what reason?
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is the most honored among the five pāramitās.
How so, Ānanda? Can a gift that is not made with the intent of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) constitute the dānapāramitā?”
Without practicing the pure precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), can one fulfill the pāramitās of śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, and dhyāna?
Ānanda said: “So it is, so it is!
O God among Gods!”
That which is "no perfection" is giving; that which is "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā) is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
That which is "no perfection" constitutes morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom; that which is "all-knowledge" is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"For this reason, among the five pāramitās, the Prajñāpāramitā is the most honored.
It is like digging the earth and scattering seeds within it; they all grow forth simultaneously."
Thus it is, Ānanda!
The *prajñāpāramitā* is that which gives birth; the five *pāramitās* and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) are accomplished through the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"For this reason, Ānanda,
the Prajñāpāramitā is the most supreme and sovereign among the five pāramitās.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has said:
‘The merits of good sons and good daughters who learn, uphold, and recite the teachings of the Prajñāpāramitā cannot be fully described.’”
The Buddha said to Kauśika:

"I have not yet finished describing the merit of those who recite [this sutra]. I am now speaking of the merit of sons and daughters of good family who write down the Prajñāpāramitā, who take up its scrolls, take refuge in them, pay homage, and serve them, making offerings of famous flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and pennants. It is of these offerings that I speak regarding their merit."
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha:

"I myself shall protect and look after these good men and good women who write out the Prajñāpāramitā, who uphold its scrolls, and who take refuge in it, making offerings and serving it with famous flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags."
The Buddha said to Kauśika:
"When good sons and good daughters recite the Prajñāpāramitā, hundreds of thousands of devas will go to their place to listen to that Dharma."
If there are those who do not understand the Dharma and wish to question the Dharma Master, as soon as they form this thought,
by virtue of this Dharma, each shall attain understanding at that very moment.
These sons and daughters of good family will then obtain the hearing of the Dharma in the present.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family preaches the Prajñāpāramitā among the fourfold assembly of disciples, their mind will be entirely without hesitation, and even if they are subjected to physical trials, they shall never fear."
"Why is this? Because they are protected by the Prajñāpāramitā, those who would test them will immediately depart.
The Buddha said:

"I do not see anything that constitutes the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); how much less could I wish to test the form of the perfection of wisdom? It is simply that I am unable to see it, for I have been subdued by the perfection of wisdom."
No one will dare to treat these good sons and good daughters with contempt, nor will their minds harbor any fear or dread.
These good sons and good daughters shall fully behold the dharmas of merit they have performed in the present.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family respects and loves their parents, śramaṇas, practitioners of the Way, friends, brothers, kinsmen, and relatives—both those within and without—and if at times someone wishes to speak ill of them, they shall explain the matter for them by upholding the Middle Way Dharma."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
A son of good family or a daughter of good family shall thereby obtain the dharmas of merit performed in the present.
Moreover, Kauśika!"

Good sons and good daughters who write out the Prajñāpāramitā and maintain this written scroll—those gods and humans above the Four Heavenly Kings who seek the Buddha-way shall come to that place to inquire after their well-being, listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, perform prostrations, circumambulate it, and then depart.

The devas among the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who seek the path of the Buddha shall go to that place to inquire after his well-being, listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, perform prostrations and circumambulations, and then depart.

The various devas in the heavens above who seek the path of the Buddha shall go to that place to pay their respects, listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, perform prostrations and circumambulations, and then depart.
These good sons and good daughters should know this in their hearts:

from incalculable, asankhyeya Buddha-fields, devas, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans will come to this place to inquire after [the Bodhisattva], to hear and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, and having paid homage and circumambulated [him], they will each depart.
This itself constitutes giving.

Those among the devas of the Tuṣita Heaven who seek the Buddha-way should go to that place to inquire after [the Bodhisattva], listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, perform prostrations and circumambulations, and then depart.

The devas among the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven who seek the path of the Buddha shall go there to inquire after [the Buddha], listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, perform prostrations and circumambulations, and then depart.

The devas dwelling in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa) who seek the path of the Buddha shall go to that place to inquire after his health, listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, perform prostrations and circumambulations, and then depart.

The Brahmakāyika devas, the Brahmapurohita devas, the Mahābrahmā devas, the Parīttābha devas, the Apramāṇābha devas, the Ābhāsvara devas, the Parīttaśubha devas, the Apramāṇaśubha devas, the Śubhakṛtsna devas, the Anabhraka devas, the Puṇyaprasava devas, the Bṛhatphala devas, the Avṛha devas, the Atapa devas, the Sudṛśa devas, the Sudarśana devas, the Akaniṣṭha devas, and all other such celestial beings shall all go to that place to pay their respects, listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, perform prostrations and circumambulations, and then each depart.
Even the gods up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven will constantly descend;
how much more so, Kauśika,

will the gods of the desire realm and the gods of the form realm from the trichiliocosm all come to inquire after [the Bodhisattva], listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, perform prostrations and circumambulations, and then each return to their own abodes?

Wherever these good sons and good daughters dwell, that place shall always be secure and firm, and no one shall cause them disturbance; except for the consequences of their own past karma which they have not yet exhausted, nothing else can move them.
"These sons and daughters of good family shall immediately attain the dharmas of merit in the present life, and they shall be able to know when the devas come.
Śakra Devānām Indra asked:
"How so, O God among Gods?"
"How shall these sons and daughters of good family know when the devas arrive to listen to, receive, serve, make offerings to, and pay homage [to them]?
The Buddha said:

"Sons and daughters of good family, if they see a radiance, they will know that devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or gandharvas have come to listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, to serve it, and to pay homage; their hearts will be filled with joy and exultation, knowing that [the beings] have indeed come."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a son or daughter of good family has never before smelled a fragrance, or if they smell a fragrance, they should know that a spirit (yakṣa) has already arrived."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Good sons and good daughters should purify their bodies.
Because they are clean and pure, the spirits and deities will all rejoice greatly and frequently go to where they are."
That person leaps for joy, like a minor deity departing as a great deity arrives; by this analogy, his majestic spiritual power is most sublime, and his radiance is towering and magnificent.

These sons and daughters of good family will always dwell in joy and purity; illness shall never take hold of their bodies, they will always find peace and security wherever they stay, and they shall never experience bad dreams.
In the dream, nothing else was seen; only the Buddha was seen;
only the stūpa was seen;
and only the Prajñāpāramitā was heard.
One sees only the tree beneath which the Buddha sits;
one sees only the turning of the Wheel of Dharma;
one sees only the moment he is about to attain Buddhahood.
One sees only the various Buddhas who, having attained Buddhahood, turn the wheel of Dharma;
one sees only the various bodhisattvas;
and one sees only the teaching of the six pāramitās in their various forms for the sake of liberating wisdom.
They see only those who shall become Buddhas;
they see only other Buddha-fields;
they hear only the sublime Dharma of the Buddhas.

One merely sees, in such-and-such a direction and such-and-such a land, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded by several hundreds of thousands of disciples and several billions of disciples, preaching the Dharma therein.
"Kauśika, this is so:

when a son of good family or a daughter of good family has seen [this] in a dream, they will immediately become peaceful; upon waking, their body will feel light, they will no longer crave food, and their body will feel as if it has been satiated by eating soft and delicious food."

It is as if a bhikṣu who has attained dhyāna, having awakened from that dhyāna, finds his mind supple and well-disposed; he does not crave food greatly, yet he is naturally satisfied by its subtle excellence.
Thus it is, Kauśika!
These sons and daughters of good family, having awakened from that state, do not think much about food; they perceive their own bodies as soft, supple, and as if fully satiated.
Why is this, Kauśika?
Malevolent spirits and ghosts will not dare to approach them.

Because these good sons and good daughters have personally witnessed the qualities of their present merit and have studied and recited the *Prajñāpāramitā*, even if they do not recite it after having transcribed it, merely by holding the scripture, taking refuge in it, paying homage, and serving it with offerings of famous flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags; [they shall obtain such merit].
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Suppose there were a full measure of the relics of the Tathāgata within Jambudvīpa, or else the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra—of these two, which would you wish to take?"
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"I would rather take the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?"
I do not dare to fail to revere the śarīra.
O God among Gods!
It is because these śarīras have emerged from the Prajñāpāramitā that they receive such offerings.

Just as I alone maintain my seat among the devas, even when I am not upon it, whenever any deva or human approaches, they all attend to me, treat me as their seat, pay homage to me, and depart immediately after receiving my instructions.
This emergence of the Prajñāpāramitā is like the emergence of the relics of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha from the Heaven among Heavens; it is born from the wisdom of sarvajñatā.
"Even if the Jambudvīpa were filled with the *tathāgata*-śarīras, O God among Gods!

And even if one part consisted of the *śarīras* filling the entire trichiliocosm, while the second part consisted of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, I would take the *Prajñāpāramitā* from between these two parts."
Why is this? Because the śarīra has emerged from within it, and by its own arrival, it receives offerings.
It is like a person in debt, O God among Gods!
Being well-acquainted with the king, he received his profound respect and affection;
there was no one to question him, nor did he have anything to fear. Why was this?
Because they obtain power from being in the presence of the King,
O God among Gods!
Since the śarīras emerge from the Prajñāpāramitā, one thereby makes offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā.
It is just as when a king resides, those who dwell in his vicinity are immediately honored by others.
The relics of the Tathāgata are born from *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge); thus, they receive offerings as that *sarvajñatā*-wisdom of the God among Gods.
One should know that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha emerges from the Prajñāpāramitā;
between these two, I choose the Prajñāpāramitā.
One who receives and upholds the Prajñāpāramitā is like a priceless maṇi jewel.
O God among Gods!
Wherever this treasure exists, there is nothing equal to it.
Wherever this is worn, ghosts and spirits shall find no opportunity and cannot cause them harm.
Whether it be men or women, great or small, if anyone is possessed by malevolent spirits, by wearing this maṇi jewel upon their body, those ghosts and spirits will immediately flee.
If one suffers from fever, by placing this maṇi jewel upon the body, the heat will be instantly dispelled.
If one suffers from wind-disorders, by holding this maṇi jewel against the body, that wind will be immediately eliminated;
if one suffers from cold, by holding this maṇi jewel against the body, the cold will no longer increase and will be removed;
if held at night in the darkness, it will illuminate everything.
If one holds a maṇi jewel in a place during the heat, that place immediately becomes very cool;
if one holds a maṇi jewel in a place during the cold, that place immediately becomes very warm;
and wherever it is placed, all poisons will not take effect.
If any man or woman, whether great or small, should be bitten by a snake or a python, if they hold this maṇi jewel against the wound, the poison will immediately depart of its own accord.
O God among Gods! This maṇi jewel is the most supreme.
If there is someone suffering from eye pain or whose vision has become dim, if they hold this maṇi jewel near their eyes, the pain will be immediately eliminated and healed.
Thus it is, O God among Gods!
The virtue of the maṇi jewel is exceedingly great and sublime.
If it is placed in water, the water immediately takes on its color.
If one takes various kinds of silk and carefully wraps a maṇi jewel therein, placing it within the water, the water immediately takes on its color;
if the water is turbid, it instantly becomes clear.
"The virtue of the maṇi jewel is beyond compare.
Ānanda asked Śakra-devānām-indra:
"How so, Kauśika?"
"There are also *maṇi* jewels in the heavens, and there are also *maṇi* jewels on the earth of Jambudvīpa; since both are equally *maṇi*, can there be any distinction between them?
He then replied to Ānanda:
"The *maṇi* jewels of the heavens are not the same as those of the human world."
Whatever exists in Jambudvīpa, its natural radiance is insufficient even to mention.
That which I have described is different from it; its virtue is exceedingly sublime, tenfold, hundredfold, thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, hundred-millionfold, and even ten-billionfold greater.
As I have said regarding the mani jewel: whether it is placed within a casket or inside a box, its radiance shines forth clearly to the outside;
even if the jewel is lifted out, the place where it was remains as bright as before.
The Prajñāpāramitā is the wisdom of sarvajña; even after the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has entered parinirvāṇa, his relics continue to receive offerings.
The relics are the vessel for the *sarvajñatā* (omniscience).
Furthermore, O God among Gods!

Suppose the three-thousandfold world system were filled with relics, and even if as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges were likewise filled with relics and combined into one portion, and the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* were made into a second portion.
I would rather take the Prajñāpāramitā from between these two portions. Why is this?
The Tathāgata was born from Sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), and his relics arose from the Prajñāpāramitā, thereby attaining for themselves the honor of being venerated.

If, O God among Gods, a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to see the Buddhas of the present in incalculable lands, they should practice in accordance with the Dharma as it is in the Prajñāpāramitā, and they should form this thought.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:

"It is so, Kauśika! In the past, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas attained Buddhahood by means of the Prajñāpāramitā; in the future, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas shall likewise attain Buddhahood by means of the Prajñāpāramitā; and the countless, asaṃkhyeya Buddhas currently residing in all the world-systems also attain Buddhahood by means of the Prajñāpāramitā."
Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Great Perfection, O God among Gods!
All people, insects, and crawling creatures—if they possess the perfections, you fully know and understand them all.”
The Buddha said,
“Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva knows this, he practices the prajñāpāramitā day and night.
Śakra-devānām-indra said:
"Why is it that one practices only the *prajñāpāramitā* and does not practice the other *pāramitās*?
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices all six *pāramitās*, yet for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, the *prajñāpāramitā* is the most honored."
If there is anything bestowed as a gift, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) surpasses it all.

One who is admonished commits no transgression; one who practices patience maintains self-restraint; one who exerts diligence is never indolent; and one who possesses single-minded concentration is not distracted. Thus perceiving all phenomena—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"Kauśika, it is like this: on the land of Jambudvīpa, there are various kinds of trees with many different colors;
each has different leaves, different flowers, different fruits, and different seeds, yet their shadows do not differ—they are all entirely similar to one another."
Thus it is, Kauśika!
The five pāramitās emerge from the prajñāpāramitā toward sarvajñatā; they mutually support one another in various ways, being no different from it.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O God among Gods! There is no virtue more supreme and majestic than the Prajñāpāramitā."
Its merit is incalculable; nothing surpasses the *prajñāpāramitā*.
O God among Gods!
There is no *pāramitā* that has already been completed.
O God among Gods!

If there is one who writes out the *Prajñāpāramitā*, upholds its scrolls, takes refuge in it, pays homage, and serves it, making offerings of famous flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags; and if there is another who likewise writes out the *Prajñāpāramitā* and bestows it as a gift upon others—of these two, which would have the greater merit?
The Buddha said,
“Ask freely, Kauśika!
Answer as you wish.”

If there are those who personally make offerings to the relics of the Tathāgata, and further distribute them to others so that they may also make offerings, while among them there are others who personally make offerings to the relics but do not distribute them to others—of these two, whose merit is greater?
Śakra Devānām Indra said: "O God among Gods!
If these sons or daughters of good family personally make offerings to the relics and further distribute them to others, their merit will far exceed that of the former."
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Kauśika!"

Good sons and good daughters, if they were to transcribe the Prajñāpāramitā, uphold its scrolls, take refuge in them, pay homage, and serve them; and if they were to offer them famous flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and pennants; and furthermore, if they were to transcribe the scrolls and distribute them to others so that those others might also make offerings to them—their merit would be exceedingly great.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Wherever a Dharma-preacher goes, if he immediately preaches the sutras and teachings to others, his merit is exceedingly great, exceedingly great."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Suppose all the people of Jambudvīpa were good men and good women, and you caused them all to uphold the ten wholesome paths of action.
What do you think, Kauśika?"
"Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied,
"It would be very great, very great!"
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as [meritorious] as a good man or a good woman who writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, takes the scripture and gives it to others so that they may write it, or reads it for others; the latter's merit is many times greater."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Setting aside Jambudvīpa, the four continents, the various small thousand-world systems, the intermediate two-thousand-world systems, and the great trichiliocosm, even if all the people throughout as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand along the Ganges were all good sons and good daughters, and you caused them all to uphold the ten wholesome paths of action."
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"Very much, very much!
O God among Gods," the Buddha said.

“Good sons and good daughters who write down the Prajñāpāramitā, or who provide a scroll of the sutra to others so that they may write it, or who read it for others, will have merit many times greater.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Suppose all the people of Jambudvīpa were good men and good women, and you caused them all to practice the four dhyānas, the four truths, the four bases of psychic power, and the five supernormal powers."
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It would not be as meritorious for a son or daughter of good family to merely write out the Prajñāpāramitā and hold the scroll themselves; rather, their merit is many times greater and more abundant if they give the scroll to others so that they may write it, or if they read it for others."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Setting aside Jambudvīpa, the four continents, and the trichiliocosm, even if all the people throughout as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand along the Ganges were all good sons and good daughters, and you caused them all to practice the four dhyānas, the four truths, the four bases of psychic power, and the five supernormal powers, and caused them all to achieve perfection therein."
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"Very much, very much,
O God among Gods!
the Buddha said.

"It is not as good as for a son of good family or a daughter of good family to write out the Prajñāpāramitā, to take this scroll and give it to others so that they may write it, or to read it for others; their merit will be many times greater."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If there is someone who reads the Prajñāpāramitā and further teaches others to study it, their merit will be many times greater."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If there is someone who studies the Prajñāpāramitā for themselves and further explains its wisdom to others, the merit they obtain will be many times greater."
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How, O God among Gods, does one who studies the Prajñāpāramitā understand wisdom within the midst [of phenomena]?"
The Buddha said:
"For those who do not understand, one should explain it to them.

If there are sons or daughters of good family in the future who wish to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*; yet instead, they may encounter an evil teacher who teaches a derivative or peripheral *prajñāpāramitā*."
Śakra Devānām-indra asked the Buddha:
"What is meant by 'peripheral' Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said:
"In the future age, there will be bhikṣus who wish to study the Prajñāpāramitā but are taught perversely by evil teachers.
Śakra Devānām Indra asked,
"What constitutes being taught perversely?"
The Buddha said:

"One teaches others to study the impermanence of form, leading them to seek impermanence within form; practicing the perfection of wisdom in this way constitutes the practice of impermanence. One studies feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, seeking impermanence within consciousness; practicing the perfection of wisdom in this way constitutes the practice of impermanence."
"Kauśika! This is the peripheral Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said:

"If that person practices the cultivation of the discoloration of phenomena, seeking the impermanence of form, and cultivates the discoloration of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, seeking the impermanence within consciousness—
if one perceives such a practitioner as being possessed of wisdom, one should uphold the Prajñāpāramitā to explain it for them."
The merit thereof becomes many times greater.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Suppose there were good men and good women in Jambudvīpa who all caused [others] to attain the stage of Srotāpanna."
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious for a son or daughter of good family to merely write out the Prajñāpāramitā; rather, it is far more meritorious to take up this scripture and give it to others so that they may write it, to instruct them to study it, or to read it for them; their merit will be many times greater."
Why is this? Because the path of the srotāpanna all issues forth from the prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Setting aside Jambudvīpa, even if one were to teach all the people throughout the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, up to as many Buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges River, and cause them to attain the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin.
"Would that merit not be great?
Śakra-devānām-indra replied,
"It would be very great, indeed very great!"
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as [meritorious] as a good man or a good woman who writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, takes the scroll and gives it to others so that they may write it, teaches them to study it, or reads it for others; the merit of this is far more abundant."
Why is this? Because the merit of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) is accomplished through the hearing of the Dharma.
From within the prajñāpāramitā, one accomplishes and attains Buddhahood, and thus emerges from the path of the srotāpanna (stream-enterer).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Suppose all were to attain the paths of Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat.
Would their merit not be great?"
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"Very much, very much,
O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not as [meritorious] as when these sons or daughters of good family write out the Prajñāpāramitā, take the scroll and give it to others so that they may write it, or read it for others; their merit is exceedingly great."
For this reason, all have attained their respective [realizations] through this very Dharma;
it is brought about by this Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this so?
For the sake of the dharma of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge),
by training in the dharma of sarvajñatā, one is then able to instruct and bring to completion the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha.
Setting aside the people of Jambudvīpa, Kauśika!

And even the people of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, up to the people of as many Buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges—suppose one were to teach all these sons and daughters of good family so that they might all attain the stage of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha.
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much, very much,
O World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious for a son or daughter of good family to merely write out the Prajñāpāramitā; rather, it is more so if they take this scroll and give it to others to have them copy it, instructing them to study it, or if they read it for others—their merit will be many times greater."
Why is this? It is because all [attainments] proceed from the Prajñāpāramitā and are due to the merit of the quality of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
For this reason, one attains the paths of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha.
For this reason, their merit becomes many times greater.
Furthermore, Kauśika,

it is not as good for all the people of Jambudvīpa to cause them to resolve upon the mind of a bodhisattva, as it is for a son of good family or a daughter of good family to take up a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and give it to others so that they may copy it, instructing them to study it and explaining it to them.
If one bestows upon them the scriptures of the *Avivartika* Bodhisattva, that person should study from these and enter deeply into the *prajñāpāramitā*.
One who studies and knows the *prajñāpāramitā* will increase and expand further, maintaining infinite knowledge and thereby attaining accomplishment.
For this reason, their merit becomes many times, indeed exceedingly much greater.
Setting aside the people of Jambudvīpa, O Kauśika,
and even those in as many Buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges River, suppose they all resolve their minds toward the practice of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

It is not as meritorious as for a good man or a good woman to take a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and give it to another person to have it copied, instructing them to study it and explaining its meaning to them.
Furthermore, they shall bestow upon them the scriptures of the *Avivartika* (non-retrogressive) Bodhisattvas, instructing people to study from these and enter deeply into the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Those who study and come to know the *prajñāpāramitā* will increase their understanding manifold; by maintaining this boundless wisdom, they will thereby achieve accomplishment.
For this reason, their merit becomes many times greater.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Suppose all the people of Jambudvīpa were to set forth on the path toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

It is not as good as a good man or a good woman who takes up a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and gives it to another person to transcribe, explaining its wisdom for them so that they may study it.
Furthermore, if one bestows upon an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra to explain its profound wisdom, the resulting merit will be many times greater.

Setting aside the people of Jambudvīpa and the three thousandfold world system, even including all those in Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, may they all resolve their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

It is not as good as a son of good family or a daughter of good family who takes up a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and gives it to another person to have it transcribed, instructing them to study and enter into wisdom.
If one were to bestow upon an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the sake of explaining its inner wisdom, the resulting merit would be many times greater.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Suppose all the people of Jambudvīpa were made into bodhisattvas who have attained the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika) toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, according to the teaching, led them into the Prajñāpāramitā; [the latter would generate greater merit]."
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
“If among these people there should be a bodhisattva who says:
‘I wish to quickly become a Buddha,’ even if they wish to quickly become a Buddha, it is not as good as a person who enters the Prajñāpāramitā.”
"Their merit would increase manifold.

Setting aside the people of Jambudvīpa and the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, even up to the people of as many Buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges, suppose they were all like bodhisattvas who are irreversible (avaivartika) from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
If one were to instruct a son of good family or a daughter of good family to enter into the Prajñāpāramitā,
what do you think, Kauśika?
Would their merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"Very much, very much,
O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said:
"Suppose there were a bodhisattva who spoke thus from within it:
'I wish to quickly become a Buddha.'"
"Even if one were to quickly become a Buddha, it would not equal the merit of one who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā and bestows it upon others;
the latter's merit is many times greater.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, so it is! O God among Gods!
Those who are supremely at peace are indeed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas; they now sit near the Buddha, receiving robes, food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for healing as they are due."
It is not as meritorious as teaching others the Prajñāpāramitā; its merit is many times greater.
Why is this? O God among Gods!
"Those who have attained the Prajñāpāramitā now sit near the Buddha.
Subhūti said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Kauśika! One should regard the śrāvakas as being among the venerable disciples, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it is because of them that the śrāvakas attain their realization.
Since these people do not seek the Buddha-way, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not train in their path. Without training in these dharmas, one cannot become a Buddha.
By training in accordance with the suchness of the Dharma, one will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and thereby reach Buddhahood.
