Chapter Four: Skillful Means (Upāyakauśalya).
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed Subhūti:

"If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who encourages and assists others in creating merit—superior to those who practice giving, uphold the precepts, and maintain self-restraint—their merit becomes even more exalted and supreme; no merit surpasses that of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s encouragement and assistance."
Subhūti said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:

"Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have performed meritorious deeds in the presence of the Buddhas of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands; in each and every land, there are Buddhas whose number cannot be reckoned, who have entered parinirvāṇa. From the moment they first resolved their minds until they reached *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attained *abhisambuddha*, and even until they entered parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder, they subsequently reach the exhaustion of the Dharma."
The merit produced therein is a perfection of merit that knows no limit.

Thus, while the śrāvakas practice giving, maintain the precepts, and exercise self-restraint to cultivate blessings, they do so with the aim of reaching the state of *anupadhiśeṣa* (nirvana without remainder) through their remaining merit.

Whatever merits have been performed by all Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa therein—extending to their body of pure precepts, body of samādhi, body of wisdom, body of liberation, and body of the vision of liberated wisdom—[all these he dedicates].

The Buddha-dharma is the ultimate great compassion. The teachings expounded by the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, are incalculable; within those teachings, one further studies all possible merits. Even if one were to calculate and aggregate all the merits produced through the Buddha-dharma of parinirvāṇa, the merit of exhortation and assistance is supreme.

To be the ultimate among all various virtues is to provide supreme encouragement and assistance; this is what constitutes encouragement and assistance. Through such encouragement and assistance, one upholds and practices for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and thereby attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Setting aside this person who is a bodhisattva—one who maintains the mind and is able to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—it is only when such a thought arises that they desire to obtain something.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:
"It is by not seeking in this way that one is able to attain anything.

Those who harbor such conceptualizations are considered unwise; yet they are able to give rise to such thoughts, and through those conceptualizations they feel regret and turn back, and through their faith they feel regret and turn back."

However, because they lack wisdom, they fall back into the four inversions—perceiving the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, the empty as substantial, and the selfless as having a self—and for this reason, their thoughts regress toward regret, their minds regress toward regret, and their faith regresses toward regret.
A bodhisattva should not form a mind that seeks anything; since there is no locus for what is sought, how could one seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:
"One should not speak these words in the presence of newly initiated bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Why is this?"
If they lack faith, lack delight, lack joy, and lack practice, they will consequently fall away.
One should speak to such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are capable of hearing [this teaching] and who dwell in the presence of virtuous teachers.

When one is able to preach this for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who hears it without fear, terror, or dread, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to provide encouragement and assistance, thereby creating merit and attaining sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
While maintaining the mind and providing such encouragement, the mind itself is also extinguished.
Since there is nothing that exists and nothing that can be perceived, what kind of mind could possibly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"With what kind of mind should one act?
The mind has no duality; it is through the natural spontaneity of the mind that one is able to act.
Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti:
“Newly initiated bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, upon hearing this, may become afraid or terrified.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to cultivate merit, how should they encourage and assist others in their blessings so as to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
Subhūti said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:

"One should provide protection against all evils destroyed by the Buddhas and sever craving and desire; practicing with equanimity as one, subduing the works of Māra, and casting off the heavy burden, then all toil and suffering will be completely exhausted. Through this knowledge, one is liberated, and the mind follows accordingly."

Regarding the merit and blessings performed by those who have entered parinirvāṇa in incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands, as well as the merit performed among the śrāvakas—if one were to calculate and sum them all together—the act of exhortation and assistance is supreme; among all kinds of virtues, none surpasses exhortation and assistance.

As for those who provide encouragement, they are able to offer such encouragement; by means of this encouragement, they maintain the practice toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. What is this "thought of non-retrogression" of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, wherein what is believed does not lead to regret or regression?

Even if a bodhisattva mahāsattva maintains the mind to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet that mind is free from any conceptualization, then this bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Even if one’s mental attention is self-aware, this constitutes a regression from perception, a regression from the mind, and a regression from what is trusted.
Even if one’s mental attention further knows that very mind, that is an act; this constitutes a regression from perception and a regression from trust.
Even if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintains mindfulness and understands, they should cultivate this awakening: "I know the exhaustion [of phenomena]; I know that there is nothing to be known.
One should understand which mind performs an action, and one should thoroughly understand the mind—that is, which mental factors perform an action upon phenomena.
That which accords with the Dharma is to act in accordance with the Dharma;
such action is not false action, for it is the work performed by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who [dedicate] the merit made by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
or the merit made by all śrāvakas, down to ordinary worldlings; or the merit made by animals who have heard the Dharma;

as well as the merit made by those among the devas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans who have heard the Dharma and have resolved their minds [upon awakening]; [if they dedicate all this merit...]"

Furthermore, for those who have newly begun to study the Bodhisattva path, it is considered supreme to calculate, combine, and accumulate [merit]; since those who provide encouragement can indeed provide such encouragement, they are therefore most venerable.
Among all various virtues, there is none that surpasses exhortation and assistance.

Therefore, that which ought to be exhorted and assisted is exhortation and assistance; it can produce the merit of exhortation and assistance, which is employed for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Even if one were to practice in this way for the sake of the dharma of exhaustion—the dharma that is neither produced nor extinguished, the dharma that has no abiding place and no arising—one would thereby attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This Dharma does not fail to understand the Dharma; because it is employed for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is without conceptualization and without regretful turning back; the mind likewise does not regretfully turn back, and that which is believed does not regretfully turn back.
Acting thus without seeking anything is that which is beyond the reach of all others; this is what is performed for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not clearly and thoroughly understand how to perform meritorious deeds.
Why is this? Because the body is illusory, and the merit produced through encouragement and assistance is likewise illusory.

The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands that what is illusory has no substantial existence; therefore, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, even if they perform meritorious deeds in the presence of Buddhas who have entered Parinirvāṇa and maintain these merits with the desire to achieve their goal, such knowledge is naturally able to bring about Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—the state of all Buddhas, the Gods among Gods.
The notions of attachment and non-attachment have already ceased in the past; furthermore, there is no notion that does not constitute a notion. To form such a notion is to lack virtue.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means); those who have not yet attained the *prajñāpāramitā* cannot enter [this state], whereas only those who have attained the *prajñāpāramitā* can enter.
Do not create for the body the existence of cognitive activity that is subject to cessation; for this reason, there is no such thing as a body.
For one who possesses the virtues of the body, the presence of conceptualization constitutes an obstruction, which conversely leads to suffering.
Abiding in the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, one does not train in performing such meritorious deeds or encouraging others to do so. Why is this?
Because it is incorrect.
To regard the Buddha in parinirvāṇa as being subject to conceptualization is, for that reason, an obstruction.
Consequently, the merit one has cultivated will not reach its fulfillment; instead, one will desire to dwell in suffering.
That which is free from conceptualization is the virtue of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
that which involves conceptualization is like a mixture of poison.
Why is this? Suppose one were to prepare delicious food and place poison within it; its color would be exceedingly fine and its fragrance such that there would be none who did not rejoice.
Unaware that there is poison in the food, the ignorant and deluded person eats it, feeling joyful and fully satiated.
When the desire for food has subsided, it remains uncomfortable for a long time.

It is extremely difficult for one who does not recognize virtuous conduct; such a person does not understand how to provide protection, does not understand the internal matter, and is unable to comprehend or know [the truth].
To speak of one who performs such virtuous deeds is like speaking of food mixed with poison. Good son!

Regarding the Buddhas of the past, future, and present—their body of precepts, their body of samādhi, their body of wisdom, their body of liberation, and their body of the vision of liberated wisdom—as well as the merits performed among the śrāvakas and those spoken of by the Buddha, the God among Gods, and furthermore the merits performed among the pratyekabuddhas, he encourages and assists them all.
If one encourages others to take hold of this merit and apply it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
yet conceives of that which is performed as a mental object (*saṃjñā*), for this reason it is like a mixture of poison.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this way:
"What are the merits of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present?
How should one provide encouragement and assistance to cultivate merit so as to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"

When this bodhisattva follows the teachings of the Tathāgata, this constitutes the cultivation of wisdom. It is spontaneously produced from the merits of the Buddha and encompasses all that pertains to the perception of phenomena. By upholding these merits to provide encouragement and assistance, and through that encouragement and assistance, they personally attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices such giving, they commit no transgression and shall never be separated from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
All that the Buddha speaks is ultimate truth.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice giving in this manner:

as pure precepts, as samādhi, as wisdom, as liberation, and as the vision of liberation through wisdom; as being without the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm; and as being without the past, future, or present, and as being non-existent. Even the gift of that which is non-existent is itself non-existent.
When one performs such giving, it is done in accordance with the Dharma; yet even the Dharma is non-existent.
The giver acts for the sake of fulfillment, and that which is given is free from poison.
One who performs a different kind of giving performs a perverse form of giving.

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices giving in accordance with the Dharma, it is known by the Buddha, the God among Gods; this very giving constitutes the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
Acting in such a manner as a Buddha—
this is precisely what constitutes the giving of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Throughout the people of the trichiliocosm, there is none whose mind of universal compassion and impartial protection is superior to his.
The supreme gift bestowed by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is that which is most honored.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
suppose all the people of the trichiliocosm were to become anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Suppose all the people in Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to provide this bodhisattva with offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick, continuing such offerings for eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, making these gifts according to whatever they themselves delighted in.
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Would that merit not be great?
Subhūti replied:
“Extremely many, extremely many!
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
“The merit of exhortation and assistance is such that its blessings surpass those mentioned above and cannot be calculated.
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“As for the merit of one who takes another’s place in exhortation, even Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges could not fully contain it.”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"

If there is a bodhisattva who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, whatever acts of giving they perform will surpass their original acts of giving; for by means of the peerless encouragement and assistance of that which is superior to what was given, it exceeds it a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, and even a hundred-billionfold.
At that time, twenty thousand devas from the heavens of the Four Great Kings all touched their heads to the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This is a most magnificent gift.”
O God among Gods!
It is through the *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva that they perform such giving; its merit is exceedingly great and sublime. Why is this?
"This is because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā* and provides encouragement and support therein.

Then the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven took celestial flowers, famous incenses, powdered incense, blended incenses, unguents, burning incenses, celestial silks, flower-canopies, banners, pennants, and musical instruments, and used them to make offerings to and delight the Buddha.
Having made their offerings, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This is a most magnificent gift,
O God among Gods!"
It is through the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva that such giving is performed, which constitutes the merit of the most supreme gift. Why is this?
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā* and provides encouragement and assistance therein.

The devas of the Salt Heaven, holding celestial flowers, renowned incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, and burning incense, as well as celestial silks, flower canopies, banners, pennants, and music, used these to make offerings to and delight the Buddha.
Having made these offerings, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This is a most magnificent gift,
O God among Gods!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such giving through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), it constitutes a merit of supreme greatness. Why is this?
Because that bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā* and provides encouragement and assistance therein.

The devas and humans of the Tuṣita Heaven offered worship and entertainment to the Buddha with celestial flowers, renowned incense, powdered incense, blended incense, fragrant unguents, burning incense, celestial silken banners, flower canopies, pennants, and musical performances.
Having made these offerings, they all spoke thus:
"This is a most magnificent gift!
O God among Gods!"
The bodhisattva mahāsattva, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), performs such giving; it is a merit of supreme greatness. Why is this?
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā* and provides encouragement and assistance therein.

The devas of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven held celestial flowers, famous incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, and burning incense, as well as celestial silks, flower canopies, banners, pennants, and musical instruments, using them to make offerings to and entertain the Buddha.
Having made these offerings, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This is a most magnificent gift,
O God among Gods!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such giving through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), it constitutes a most supreme and venerable merit. Why is this?
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā* and provides encouragement and assistance therein.

The devas of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven took celestial flowers, renowned incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, burning incense, celestial silks, flowered canopies, banners, and musical instruments, and used them to make offerings to and delight the Buddha.
Having made these offerings, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is a most magnificent gift,
O God among Gods!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such giving through *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), it constitutes a most supreme and honored merit. Why is this?
Because that bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā* and provides encouragement and assistance therein.

The Brahmā gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, the Puṇyaprasava gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Avṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, the Akaniṣṭha gods, and all other devas, with their heads bowed at the Buddha’s feet, all said:
“Excellent!”
O God among Gods!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the prajñāpāramitā, it constitutes the merit of a most great giving. Why is this?
"This is because that bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the prajñāpāramitā and provides encouragement and assistance therein.
The Buddha said to the devas of Śuddhāvāsa:
"Set aside the bodhisattva mahāsattvas within a trichiliocosm."

Furthermore, suppose all the people in Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to become *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* [Buddhas]; and suppose there were again people in Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who together provided these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with offerings of fine garments, food and drink, bedding for coming and going, and medicinal requisites for illness—all such offerings for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, giving whatever they delighted in, or even exceeding this.

It does not equal the gift of encouragement and assistance made by a bodhisattva mahāsattva; nor does it equal the merit performed by those who are included within the pure body of precepts, the body of samādhi, the body of wisdom, the body of liberation, and the body of the vision of liberated wisdom of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as the bodies of all the śrāvakas—were one to calculate and sum them all together, they would not equal the gift of encouragement or the one who encourages, for this is supremely honored and unsurpassed.
"By providing such encouragement and assistance, one thereby upholds the path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one were to calculate and sum up all that has been taught by the World-Honored One, there is nothing more supreme than this encouragement and assistance."
[They] all provide encouragement and assistance; having provided encouragement and assistance, what dharma does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva obtain from this?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“A person of the Way and its Virtue should know that regarding the dharmas of the past, future, and present, there is nothing to be grasped and nothing to be relinquished, and there is neither anything to be known nor anything to be attained.”
That which is the Dharma is unarisen, and the Dharma is also unceasing.
The Dharma does not arise from anywhere, nor does the Dharma cease from anywhere.
Within the Dharma, there is absolutely no arising; the Dharma likewise does not cease from having existed.
This is the dharma that accords with the dharma.
I encourage and assist it on their behalf; this is what is meant by encouragement and assistance.
One who practices such giving will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, Subhūti, the exhortation and assistance [of others] by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is supreme.
Furthermore, Subhūti:

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in the presence of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, acts as a substitute for those who practice giving and encourages them; he acts as a substitute for those who maintain morality, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom, and encourages them; he acts as a substitute for those who have attained liberation and encourages them; and he acts as a substitute for those who have attained the vision of the body through the wisdom of liberation, and encourages them.

To act as a substitute in exhorting and assisting those who are liberated is giving; those who are liberated are patience; those who are liberated are diligence; those who are liberated are single-mindedness; those who are liberated are wisdom; those who are liberated are the wisdom of liberation; those who are liberated are the body seen by the wisdom of liberation; those who are liberated are that which is liberated; those who are liberated act as substitutes in exhorting and assisting; and those who are liberated are the Dharma.

Therefore, there has never been anyone in the future who has attained liberation such as this; those who have attained liberation among the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, currently residing in incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands, are precisely the disciples of the Buddhas.
Those who are liberated are the disciples of the Buddhas of the past; those who are liberated are the disciples of the Buddhas of the present.
Within this Dharma there is neither bondage nor attachment nor liberation. Such a Dharma is maintained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Among all such acts of giving, there is none that can surpass this, nor any that can destroy it.
Subhūti, this is the supreme act of a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s encouragement and assistance.

Suppose, Subhūti, that in as many buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges River, every bodhisattva therein lived for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges River; and suppose that every person in those as many buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges River were to provide all those bodhisattva mahāsattvas with offerings of fine garments, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick, continuing thus for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges River. Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose they all maintained the precepts and practiced patience, were untiring in their vigor, and attained samādhi in meditation—yet even if they did so a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, or even many hundreds of millions of times over, it would not equal the merit and virtue of the act of encouragement and assistance, which is the most supreme and excels above them all.
5. Hell Chapter. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Hell Chapter, Fifth. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā accomplishes much.”
O God among Gods!
Because of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is no name that cannot be attained.
O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the ultimate illumination.
O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā dispels darkness.
O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā is without attachment.
O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme,
O God among Gods!
For those who are sightless, the Prajñāpāramitā acts as their eyes.
O God among Gods!
For those who are deluded, the Prajñāpāramitā bestows the path.
O God among Gods!
That which is sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) is precisely the prajñāpāramitā.
O God among Gods!
The prajñāpāramitā is the mother of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
O God among Gods!
That which is neither produced nor extinguished is precisely this Prajñāpāramitā.
O God among Gods!
Endowed with the three aspects of the twelvefold wheel of Dharma, one turns this Prajñāpārāmitā.
O God among Gods!
This Prajñāpārāmitā brings complete peace and security to all who are afflicted.
O God among Gods!
Prajñāpāramitā provides protection within birth and death.
O God among Gods!
Since the perfection of wisdom is entirely spontaneous with respect to all phenomena,
how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell within this perfection of wisdom?
“O God among Gods!
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“The world is sustained by the *sūtra* because it abides in the *prajñāpāramitā*; therefore, those who revere the Buddha should take refuge in the *prajñāpāramitā*.”
Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself,
"For what reason has the Venerable Śāriputra posed this question?
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed Śāriputra:
“For what reason does the Venerable One ask such a question?
Śāriputra said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
“Kauśika!...”

The perfection of wisdom is the protection of the bodhisattva; by means of its supportive merit and blessings, it brings about omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), surpassing the bodhisattva’s other practices, such as giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration.

It is like a person who has been blind since birth; whether there be a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or even a million such people, if they have no guide, they will be unable to reach their destination.
If one wishes to enter a city, one does not know how one should proceed.

In the same way, Kauśika, the five *pāramitās* are like the blind who see nothing; separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*, they likewise do not know how to proceed when wishing to enter into *sarvajñatā*.
The perfection of wisdom is the protection of the five perfections, providing them all with eyes.
The perfection of wisdom is that which protects, enabling the five perfections each to obtain their respective names.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha:
“How should one maintain oneself when entering into the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"Form is not seen as having an entry point; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also not seen as having entry points. To view the five aggregates in this way, without seeing an entry point, is to guard the *prajñāpāramitā*."
“If it is so, O God among Gods!
This constitutes guarding the Prajñāpāramitā.
By guarding it in this manner, what dharma does one attain?”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“To have nothing to guard is itself the attainment of the guarding of the Dharma; it is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Prajñāpāramitā does not reach omniscience (sarvajñatā), nor can it be reached; it is not reached by guarding, nor is anything reached within birth and death."
"How, O God among Gods, should one attain it?
The Buddha said:
"Because there is nothing to be attained, one is able to attain.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"Few indeed are those who can equal you, O God among Gods!"
"Just as with all dharmas in the Prajñāpāramitā, since all dharmas are neither produced nor extinguished, where could they abide? There is no abiding.
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"If a bodhisattva at any time forms such a thought, he then departs from the Prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If there is a cause, one should then bring to mind the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Knowing that the *prajñāpāramitā* is empty and non-existent, neither near nor far—this is therefore the *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"In what dharma does the perfection of wisdom place its faith?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"One who has faith in the *prajñāpāramitā* does not believe in form (*rūpa*), nor do they believe in feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*).
They have no belief in the path of the *srotāpanna*, nor do they believe in the paths of the *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, or *pratyekabuddha*."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods! That which is called the Mahāsattva-pāramitā is none other than the Prajñāpāramitā.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“How is it known that the *mahāsattva-pāramitā* is due to this *prajñāpāramitā*, Subhūti?”
Regarding form, there is neither great nor small; one does not take form as a witness, nor does one act as a witness for form.

Regarding sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is likewise neither great nor small; one does not take consciousness as a witness, nor does one act as a witness for consciousness.
Thus, one attains the ten powers of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and is no longer weak;
omniscience (sarvajñatā) is neither broad nor narrow.
Why is this? Because omniscience (sarvajñatā) is neither expansive nor narrow, one knows that there is no practice within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is that?
The perfection of wisdom is non-existent.
If there were anything to be sought therein— whether a person or something that exists— what could it be?
This would be a great error. Why?
Because persons have no place of birth; both the person and the prajñāpāramitā are equally spontaneous (svabhāva).
Because persons are illusory and fleeting, both the person and the Prajñāpāramitā are incalculable.
The person is not destroyed, and the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
One who understands that the person is like the Prajñāpāramitā shall attain supreme, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
"Because humans also possess power, the Tathāgata manifests as possessing power.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is most profound, most profound!"
"O God among Gods!
If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has faith in the *prajñāpāramitā*, who does not speak of its shortcomings nor harbor any doubt, from where has such a person come to be born in this world?"
"Since beginning their practice of the bodhisattva path, how many have heard and understood the matters of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and how many have entered into it according to the teaching?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"They have come from other buddha-fields to be born here."
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has made offerings to the Buddhas in other directions and has heard the *prajñāpāramitā* from their bestowal of prophecy,
by hearing the *prajñāpāramitā* once again, he reflects to himself:
"I am no different from seeing the Buddha in person."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Can the Prajñāpāramitā be seen or heard?
The Buddha said:
"It cannot be seen.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since this bodhisattva has practiced in accordance with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, for how long has he been hearing it?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"These are not of one kind of training; each has respectively made offerings to several hundreds or several thousands of Buddhas and has beheld them all, and under them all they have practiced pure precepts."
If there are those who, upon hearing the *prajñāpāramitā* amidst the assembly, abandon it and depart, they show no reverence for the Dharma of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
When the Buddha teaches the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, such persons abandon it and do not wish to hear it.
Why is this? Because in their previous lives these people heard the Prajñāpāramitā and yet abandoned it.
Furthermore, they do not apply themselves with body or mind; all of this is brought about by those who are ignorant.
Because of these offenses, if they hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they further obstruct others and prevent them from teaching it.
To obstruct the *prajñāpāramitā* is to obstruct omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
To obstruct omniscience (sarvajñatā) is to obstruct the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

Because of this sin of obstructing the Dharma, one shall die and enter the great hells for hundreds of thousands of years, even hundreds of millions of years, where one must endure various hellish poisons and pains that are beyond description.
When their lifespan there is exhausted, they are reborn in a mahānaraka hell in another direction;
when that lifespan is again exhausted, they transmigrate further to be born in a mahānaraka hell in yet another direction.
Śāriputra said to the Buddha,
"Does that sin cause one to fall into the five heinous crimes?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Though their transgressions are illustrated by metaphors, they cannot be fully compared.
If, when reciting, chanting, or reading the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds harbor doubts regarding the Dharma and they are unwilling to study it, thinking:
'These words were not spoken by the Tathāgata.'"
He stops others from speaking, saying, "Do not learn this.
This is to ruin oneself and further ruin others; having drunk the poison oneself, one then makes others drink it as well.

These people have already brought about their own ruin and loss, and they further cause others to be lost; not understanding the profound *prajñāpāramitā* themselves, they go on to corrupt others as well.
Such people as these should not be seen. Śāriputra!
One should not sit, rise, speak, or eat and drink together with them.
Why is this? Such people who slander the Dharma dwell in darkness themselves, and furthermore, they lead others into darkness.
These individuals poison and destroy their own bodies; they are no different from those who sever the Dharma.
If there is one who has faith in what is spoken and acts upon those words, the person’s incurred transgression shall be equal and no different [from that of the speaker]. Why is this?
Because they have slandered the words of the Buddha.
"One who slanders the Prajñāpāramitā has, in effect, slandered all dharmas.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that you will explain, what kind of form and appearance does one who slanders the Dharma receive?"
"Do you not know how large his body is?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"If those who slander the Dharma were to hear of this matter, the blood would boil and gush forth from their faces."
Fearing that he might die immediately, he was consequently seized by great agony.
Upon hearing this, the man’s heart became filled with sorrow and distress until it was utterly consumed,
just as a severed flower placed in the midday sun withers away instantly.
Śāriputra said: "I pray that you will speak of this for the sake of others, so that they may know how their bodies receive form.
It shall serve as a great illumination for future generations; those who hear it and feel awe should reflect within themselves:"
"I must not slander or reject the Dharma like that person.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"This is what is called the great illumination for showing others."

Because of their transgressions, they receive bodies that are exceedingly hideous; they dwell in places of extreme toil, suffering, and stench that are truly beyond description, where their pain is immense and lasts for a long, agonizing duration.
When these good men and good women hear these words, it will be sufficient for them to refrain from ever again slandering [the Dharma].
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"Good men and good women, hearing that such people incur this transgression merely by what they say while sitting, [will be deterred]."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“These foolish people, having become śramaṇas within my Dharma, instead slander the Prajñāpāramitā, saying:
‘This is not the Path.’”

"To cease from the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* is to cease from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. To cease from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is to sever the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present. Having severed *sarvajñatā*, one severs the Dharma. Having severed the Dharma, one severs the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus. By severing the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus, one incurs immeasurable and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sins."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O God among Gods! If there should be one who severs the prajñāpāramitā, by how many factors does this occur?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Because they have been struck by Māra, these sons of good family and daughters of good family will lack faith and find no joy.
Due to these two causes, they will be able to sever the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are four more things that sever the perfection of wisdom.
What are these four?

To follow the words of an evil teacher, not to train in accordance with them, not to uphold the ultimate Dharma, and to be intent on slandering others, seeking out their shortcomings while being self-conceited—
these are the four matters.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods, there are few who have faith in the Prajñāpāramitā,
because they do not fully understand this Dharma.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
There are few who have faith in the *prajñāpāramitā*, because they do not understand the Dharma.”
Subhūti asked:
"In what way is it that there are few who have faith in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation. Why is this?
Because the very nature of form is form.”
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of consciousness is simply consciousness.
Past form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Why? Because past form is of its own nature (*svabhāva*).
Future form is neither attached to nor bound, nor is it liberated. Why is this?
Because future form is the very nature of form.
Presently, form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation. Why is this?
Because form is the very nature of form.
Past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Why is this? Because the nature of past form is such.
Future consciousness is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Why is this? Because future consciousness is of its own nature.
Presently, consciousness is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Why is this? Because consciousness is by its very nature such.
"For this reason, Subhūti, those who have faith in the profound Prajñāpāramitā are few. 6.
Chapter on Purity. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is it because they have not familiarized themselves with it that there are so few who understand the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said to Subhūti, “So it is, so it is!”
There are few who understand the Prajñāpāramitā; this is due to the fact that they have not cultivated it through familiarity.
Why is this so, Subhūti?
Because the purity of form is also the purity of the path;
it is said that the purity of form is also the purity of the path because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also pure.
It is said that the path is also pure; therefore, consciousness is also pure.
Furthermore, Subhūti, form is pure and omniscience (sarvajñatā) is also pure, and form is also pure.
Therefore, the purity of form and the purity of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) are equal and without distinction.
Now, the former does not interrupt the latter, and the latter does not interrupt the former; thus, there is no destruction.
For this reason.
"Previously, it was not severed.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Heaven among Heavens! As for that which is pure,"
"It is profound.
The Buddha said,
"It is utterly pure."
Śāriputra said:
"Purity is the ultimate clarity,
O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said,
“It is utterly pure. Śāriputra said:
“Pure and free from defilement,
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"Extremely pure. Śāriputra said,
"Pure and free from blemish."
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
"It is exceedingly pure."
Śāriputra said:
“It is pure and non-existent,
O God among Gods!”
The Buddha said,
"It is exceedingly pure.
Śāriputra said:
“Regarding desire, there is no desire;
it is pure, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"Extremely pure. Śāriputra said:
"It is pure through the absence of form within form."
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
"It is exceedingly pure."
Śāriputra said: "O God among Gods!
That which is unarisen is form, and it is utterly pure."
The Buddha said,
"It is exceedingly pure.
Śāriputra said:
"It is exceedingly pure, O God among Gods, that there is both wisdom and the absence of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"Extremely pure. Śāriputra said:
"For one who possesses wisdom, the absence of a knower is extremely pure."
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
"It is exceedingly pure."
Śāriputra said: “O God among Gods!
That which possesses wisdom regarding form, yet is devoid of a [substantial] knower, is utterly pure.”
The Buddha said,
"It is exceedingly pure.
Śāriputra said:
“Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is neither wisdom nor lack of wisdom;
this is utter purity, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"Extremely pure. Śāriputra said:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is also extremely pure."
O God among Gods!
Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) neither increases nor decreases.
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
"It is exceedingly pure.
Śāriputra said:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is utterly pure; it takes nothing at all among all dharmas, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"Extremely pure.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The self is pure, and form is also pure."
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"It is fundamentally pure."
Subhūti said: "Therefore it is said:
'I am pure; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also pure.'"
"O God among Gods!
the Buddha said,
"It is fundamentally pure."
Subhūti said: “I am pure, and the Path is also pure,
O God among Gods!”
The Buddha said,
"Fundamentally pure. Subhūti said:
“The self is pure, and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is also pure,
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"Fundamentally pure. Subhūti said:
"The self is pure and without origin."
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
"Fundamentally pure."
Subhūti said:
"The self is pure and boundless; form, O God among Gods, is likewise pure and boundless."
The Buddha said,
“Fundamentally pure. Subhūti said:
"The self is without limit; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also without limit, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"Fundamentally pure. Subhūti said:
"That which understands purity is precisely the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
The Buddha said,
"Fundamentally pure. Subhūti said:
“O God among Gods! The Prajñāpāramitā is neither there, nor is it here; it is neither apart from this, nor is it in between.”
The Buddha said,
“Fundamentally pure.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows this, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Those who possess conceptualization have already become far removed from the perfection of wisdom."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
"Where there are words, there is conceptualization; because of conceptualization, there is attachment.
Subhūti said to the Buddha, "The Perfection is difficult to fathom, O God among Gods!"
“Peaceful stability is the resolution of attachment. Śāriputra said:
“Ask Subhūti: what constitutes attachment?”

Subhūti said: "To know that form is empty is called attachment; to know that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty is called attachment. To know past phenomena as past phenomena is called attachment; to know future phenomena as future phenomena is called attachment; to know present phenomena as present phenomena is called attachment."
"One who knows the Dharma attains great merit; for a bodhisattva who gives rise to such a thought, this itself constitutes attachment.
Śakra Devānām Indra asked Subhūti:
"What is meant by 'attachment'?"
Subhūti said: “It is known by the mind,
Kauśika!”
Holding this knowledge, one gives it as a gift and brings it to the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The mind is fundamentally pure and is capable of performing all actions.

Good sons and good daughters who are bodhisattvas exhort and instruct others toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, preach the True Dharma for them, do not lose anything within themselves, and achieve much in the lineage of the Buddhas.
"These good sons and good daughters, by being free from all attachments, abandon the fundamental limit (*mūlakoṭi*).
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Subhūti! This causes bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to know that the limit of the beginning (*pūrvakoṭi*) is a matter of attachment to awakening.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
It possesses profound and subtle qualities;
I shall now speak of it.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I wish and desire to hear it."
The Buddha said:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, forms a conceptualization and follows that which is conceived, they thereby become attached to the past, the future, and the present."

The Buddha, the God among Gods, provides sympathetic encouragement (*anumodanā*) for all dharmas without exception; this is what constitutes sympathetic encouragement toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because there is no dharma within dharmas, it is said that there is no past, future, or present.
Therefore, there is nothing that can be produced, nor can there be any conceptualization; it cannot exist through causes and conditions, nor can it be seen, heard, or known.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Its essence is profoundly deep and pure,
O God among Gods!”
The Buddha said,
“Fundamentally pure. Subhūti said:
"Now I take refuge in the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said,
"Because there is no agent in phenomena, one attains the state of an Arhat (Abhisambuddha)."
Subhūti said: “All dharmas truly do not bring about the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“There are no two dharmas; because their essence is fundamentally pure, they are said to be one. As for this purity, even within all things there is no agent.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Therefore, to be free from all attachments is to abandon the limit of beginning (pūrvakoṭi).”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to comprehend,
O God among Gods!”
The Buddha said: “It is so!
There is no one who attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
Subhūti said: "The Prajñāpāramitā is incalculable, O Devātideva!"
The Buddha said, "So it is, Subhūti!
It is not something known by the mind."
Subhūti said: "There is no agent,
O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said:
"Because there is no agent, there is nothing to which one can become attached.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How should a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said,
"To practice without conceptualizing feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is to practice the perfection of wisdom."
Form is not full of form; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Form being non-full is the practice of non-form; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not full; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is difficult to fathom, O God among Gods!
To be attached while having nothing to which one is attached—this is truly non-attachment.”
The Buddha said:
"To be unattached to form is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
To be unattached to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is to practice the perfection of wisdom."
This is the practice of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva:

they do not cling to form; they do not cling to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor do they cling to the paths of the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? Because it transcends all attachments.
Furthermore, it emerges from within omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Dharma you have taught is exceedingly profound and difficult to fathom,
O God among Gods!”
"If that which is spoken does not increase, and that which is not spoken does not decrease.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"
Subhūti! It is as if, for example, a Tathāgata were to praise emptiness for the entirety of his life—the emptiness would not increase;
nor would it decrease if he did not praise it.
For example, it is like a phantom person: even when praised, it does not increase; even when not praised, it does not decrease.
Hearing good things, it feels no joy; hearing evil things, it feels no sorrow.
"In this way, Subhūti,
though one may each recite and study these dharmas, the dharmas neither increase nor decrease.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha:
“The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva deeply detests the practice of asceticism regarding the Prajñāpāramitā.
If there is one who guards the Prajñāpāramitā, they will not be indolent, nor terrified, nor frightened; they will not waver and will not turn back.”
Why is this? Because one who guards the *prajñāpāramitā* guards emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

All should pay homage to the bodhisattva mahāsattva because he has donned the great armor (*saṃnāha*) and fights with emptiness; he dons the armor for the sake of all people, and he raises up emptiness for the sake of all people. This bodhisattva mahāsattva is supremely courageous and valiant.
"O God among Gods!
By means of the dharma of emptiness, one personally attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and achieves the state of an avaivartika Buddha.
At that time, another bhikṣu thought to himself:
"One should take refuge in the Prajñāpāramitā as that which is neither a dharma that arises nor a dharma that ceases.
Śakra-devānām-indra said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva follows the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, what teaching is he following?"
Subhūti said: "It is in accordance with the teaching of emptiness.
Śakra-devānām-indra said:
“What is it that follows the teaching of emptiness? Subhūti replied,
“Those who desire tranquility— these are the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who understand the prajñāpāramitā.”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O God among Gods! For how long should one who receives this Prajñāpāramitā be protected?"
Subhūti said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"How is it, Kauśika!
Are you able to perceive any dharma that ought to be protected?"
And yet you say you wish to protect it.
Śakra Devānām Indra said, “No.”
Subhūti said: "Those who act in accordance with the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā will thereby obtain protection.
Whether they be humans or non-humans, none shall ever find an opportunity to harm them."
Subhūti said: “If a bodhisattva mahāsattva protects emptiness, he has already been practicing in accordance with the perfection of wisdom.
How so, Kauśika?”
"Is it possible to protect an echo?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied,
"It is not possible."
Subhūti said: "It is so, Kauśika!
For a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom, that dharma is also like an echo."
Because those who know this likewise have no conceptualization, they practice the *prajñāpāramitā* by means of non-conceptualization.

Through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, Brahmā, and all the honored devas from throughout the trichiliocosm all came before the Buddha; they paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and each stood to one side.

All the celestial kings, Śakra, and Brahmā, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, perceived that all the thousand Buddhas were named Śākyamuni, that those bhikṣus were all named Subhūti, and that those who questioned about the Prajñāpāramitā were all like Śakradevendra.

Chapter Seven: On Original Non-existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods! As for all dharmas following in succession...”
This is the discourse on the Dharma; therefore, it is said that there is nothing to be diminished.

All phenomena (dharmas) have no origin; the characteristic of these phenomena is that they are unimpeded. As with the phenomenon of space, which is unborn, all that is born cannot be apprehended; because this is the arising of phenomena, there is nothing to be attained.
The various gods of the desire realm and the Brahmā deities all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Those who are thus tranquil are the disciples of the Buddha.
What the Venerable Subhūti has now spoken is entirely empty."
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"It is in accordance with the teaching of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti, how does one know that which accords with the teaching of the Tathāgata?
Subhūti replied again:
“As the Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent (mūla-abhāva), this is the teaching of the Tathāgata.
All those of the past, future, and present are likewise fundamentally non-existent.
The Buddha said:
"To follow that which is originally non-existent is to follow the teaching of the Tathāgata.
All dharmas are also originally non-existent.
Just as all dharmas are originally non-existent, the Tathāgata is also originally non-existent."
All things are originally non-existent, and all are fundamentally non-existent.
Subhūti, this is because following the teaching of the Tathāgata is without distinction.
To follow fundamental non-existence is to follow the teaching of the Tathāgata without distinction or difference.
To follow the Tathāgata is to follow original non-existence; that which is original non-existence is the Tathāgata.
To establish what Subhūti establishes is to follow the teaching of the Tathāgata.
Just as the Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent and unimpeded, so too all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent and unimpeded.
Subhūti, this is to follow the teaching of the Tathāgata.
Because the Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*), so too are all phenomena fundamentally non-existent; this single fundamental non-existence is equal and without distinction.

The self is also non-existent, the agent is fundamentally non-existent, and there is no agent either; everything is fundamentally non-existent, and yet even that fundamental non-existence is non-existent.
Just as "original non-existence" (prakṛti-niḥsvabhāva) is originally non-existent, so too is the self; therefore, Subhūti acts in accordance with the teaching of the Tathāgata.
Just as the original non-existence of the Tathāgata is not different and has no distinction, so too all dharmas are originally non-existent, not different, and have no distinction.
This is because the Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent, neither subject to destruction nor decay, and ungraspable; Subhūti, by this, follows the teaching of the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata and all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent and without distinction; there is no distinct fundamental non-existence, nor is there any separate fundamental non-existence—all are entirely and utterly fundamental non-existence.
As for those whom Subhūti follows, they enter into that which is incalculable, yet there is nothing entered; this is what it means to follow the teaching of the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*); he does not exist in the past, the future, or the present.
Since all dharmas are likewise fundamentally non-existent, they too do not exist in the past, the future, or the present.
In this way, Subhūti acts in accordance with the teaching of the Tathāgata.
That which is the "original non-existence" (prakṛti-niḥsvabhāva) of the Tathāgata is called the teaching of the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is himself original non-existence.
The future is fundamentally non-existent, the past is fundamentally non-existent, and the present is fundamentally non-existent.
Because it accords with the fundamental non-existence of the past, the teaching of the Tathāgata is this very fundamental non-existence.
Because it accords with the fundamental non-existence of the future, the teaching of the Tathāgata is fundamental non-existence.
Because it accords with the fundamental non-existence of the present, the teaching of the Tathāgata is fundamental non-existence.
Because the past, future, and present are fundamentally non-existent (*abhāva*), the teaching of the Tathāgata is this fundamental non-existence.
Because the past, future, and present are fundamentally non-existent, the teaching of the Tathāgata is this fundamental non-existence, which is equal and without distinction.
Just as all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent (*abhāva*), so too is Subhūti; they are without distinction. This is because he accords with the teaching of the Tathāgata without distinction.
This is the true fundamental non-existence of a bodhisattva, which leads him to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; furthermore, both are equally and identically fundamental non-existence.
Because he is as originally non-existent (*tathābhūta-ajāti*), he obtains the name "Tathāgata, Originally Non-existent," and the earth immediately quakes in six ways.
Since the Tathāgata attained his realization because of this original non-existence, Subhūti acts in accordance with the teaching of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if he does not follow form, nor does he follow feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; if he does not follow the path of the srotāpanna, nor does he follow the paths of the sakṛdāgāmin, the anāgāmin, the arhat, or the pratyekabuddha—this, Subhūti, is for him to follow the teaching of the Tathāgata.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The absence of intrinsic nature (*abhāva*) is profoundly deep,
O God among Gods!”
The Buddha said, “It is so;
‘original non-existence’ is truly profound.

When he spoke of original non-existence, three hundred bhikṣus all attained arhatship; five hundred bhikṣuṇīs all attained the stage of srotāpanna; five hundred devas and humans all attained the patient acceptance of the dharma that is unarisen; and sixty bodhisattvas all attained the path of arhatship.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"These bodhisattvas, having made offerings to five hundred past Buddhas, have all practiced giving, guarded the pure precepts, perfected patience, exerted diligence, and established themselves in dhyāna. Yet, because they did not attain the *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya*, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess the aspiration for the Way and enter into emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, those who are devoid of *upāyakauśalya* will instead realize the limit of reality midway and become śrāvakas."
Suppose, Śāriputra, there were a great bird whose body was four thousand li,
or eight thousand li, or twelve thousand li, or sixteen thousand li, or thirty thousand li, and it wished to descend from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the land of Jambudvīpa.
This bird has no wings, yet it descends from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven by throwing itself down.
What do you think, Śāriputra?
If this bird wished to return halfway to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, would it be able to return?
Śāriputra said: "I cannot,
O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said:
"If this bird were to descend to Jambudvīpa, wishing not to cause its body pain,
could it possibly avoid causing pain?"
Śāriputra said: "I cannot,
O God among Gods!"
When that bird descends, its body cannot help but suffer pain;
it will either die or fall into extreme distress. Why is this?
"His body is exceedingly large, yet he has no wings.
The Buddha said, "It is so, Śāriputra!"

Even if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges, practices giving, guards pure precepts, perfects patience, exerts diligence, and establishes himself in meditative concentration, and with a most vast resolve desires to encompass all things and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
One who does not possess the *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya* will fall midway into the stage of the *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, regarding the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, falsely conceives of themselves as not possessing the precepts, samādhi, wisdom, the wisdom of liberation, or the wisdom of insight of a Tathāgata, they are indeed not maintaining the precepts, samādhi, wisdom, the wisdom of liberation, or the wisdom of insight of a Tathāgata. Because they do not truly know the Tathāgata, yet claim to understand him, they merely hear an empty sound and form a conception based on what they have heard; though they maintain this desire to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they will ultimately fail to achieve it and instead fall midway into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha paths.
"Why is this? It is because they have not attained the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall what the Buddha has taught: those who are separated from the *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya* cannot themselves attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should skillfully study the prajñā-pāramitā with upāya-kauśalya.
The devas of the desire realm and the sons of the gods of the form realm all addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is profound, difficult to comprehend, and difficult to understand; those who remain indifferent shall not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Buddha spoke to the devaputras, saying:
"In this way, the Prajñāpāramitā is profound and difficult to comprehend; it is quiescent, and one cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through it."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to comprehend,
O God among Gods!”
As I contemplate this wisdom, it is one who is profoundly serene who is able to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
Because there is no one here who attains *abhisambodhi*; therefore, it is said that the dharmas are empty and unconditioned, and thus one attains *abhisambodhi*.
Because one employs the emptiness of phenomena, one cannot even apprehend that there is anyone who shall become an *anuttara-samyak-saṃbuddha*; therefore, all phenomena are empty.
That there is nothing whatsoever within phenomena is the "Dharma-word"; because there is no act of becoming an *anuttara-samyak-saṃbuddha*, it is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
There is no one who attains unconditioned *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there anyone who has attained *anuttara-samyak-sambodhi*; for they contemplate all dharmas as entirely empty.
One who follows this, O God among Gods!
"And yet, remaining serene, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and becomes an *arhat* Buddha.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"As you have described it, to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* while remaining serene is truly most difficult."
Why is this? Emptiness does not think:
"I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and become an arhat-samyak-saṃbuddha."
"A Dharma such as this makes it easy to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
How could bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, ever turn back?"
Subhūti said: "One should understand it thus:
'For one who is not serene, it is difficult to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"By means of form, does one not return to, nor realize, anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
He replied:
"No. "By returning to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, would one not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
He replied:
"No. "Is it possible that one who attains the Dharma through a different form could fail to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
He replied:
"No. "Is it possible that one could obtain the Dharma by means of a different feeling, perception, mental formation, or consciousness, and yet not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
He replied, "No. [The Buddha asked:
"Since form is originally non-existent, would you not return to it and fail to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
He replied, “No. [The Buddha asked:
“Since feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are fundamentally non-existent, would you not then turn back and fail to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
He replied, "No. How so, Śāriputra?"
"If one could have a distinct color that was originally non-existent, and having returned to the state of dharmas, were not to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? He replied, "No."

“Could it be that the fundamental nature of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is originally non-existent, such that one returns to the Dharma and does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
He replied, "No. [The Buddha asked,] "How so, Śāriputra?"
"Would one who returns to the original non-action not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? He replied, "No."
“Is it possible that what previously did not exist can now exist differently, such that one might return from the dharmas and yet fail to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? He replied, “No.”
"If one does not attain anything in this Dharma, what Dharma could there be to return from, such that one would produce *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"According to the Dharma as it has been taught, there is no bodhisattva who returns."
Subhūti said: "A bodhisattva possesses three virtues, as taught by the Tathāgata.
The first is the Buddha-vehicle (buddhayāna), wherein the bodhisattva does not calculate [the three], just as Subhūti has stated."
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Śāriputra:
"As for this 'single path' spoken of by Subhūti, you should question him about it.
Then Śāriputra addressed Subhūti:
"I wish to ask about the matter of the bodhisattva’s path of the Buddha-vehicle, which you have described as the single path. Subhūti!
I wish to ask about the matter of the bodhisattva’s path of the Buddha-vehicle, which you have described as the single path."
Subhūti said: "How is it,
Śāriputra, that within the state of original non-existence one can perceive the three paths?"
"These are the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"Within original non-existence, one does not perceive two distinct things."
Subhūti said: "How is it, Śāriputra?
Is that which is fundamentally non-existent a single thing?"
Therefore, it is called "attainment.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing that all things are fundamentally non-existent, does not allow their mind to become indolent, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly reach the stage of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”

It is exactly as described and not otherwise; all this is brought about by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha. This is what is meant by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s fundamental non-existence being without difference.
If a bodhisattva’s mind is not indolent, they will eventually attain the state of a bodhisattva.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What is meant by a bodhisattva?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"To attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is precisely this.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by 'bodhisattva-mahāsattva'?"
"If one wishes to achieve this, how should one abide?
The Buddha said:
"Regard all people as equal; let your mind be without distinction, free from any intent to harm, and direct a heart of loving-kindness toward others, remaining no different in body."

Their minds are supple; their minds are filled with compassion; their minds are free from anger, free from obstruction, and free from affliction; they regard others no differently than they would their own parents.
"This is the mind in which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwell;
you should train yourself in this way.
Chapter 8: The Chapter on the Non-Retrogressive (Avinivartanīya) from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How should one compare, observe, and examine the marks and conduct of an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva, so as to know that this is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"Regarding ordinary people, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even the stages of the path of a tathāgata, upon hearing that they are all fundamentally non-existent, one remains unshaken and without distinction."
Within those dharmas, there is likewise primordial non-existence (*ādi-anutpāda*); this is what is meant by primordial non-existence within immovability.
This is itself deliverance.
As it has been heard, one does not turn back nor harbor doubt; one neither asserts "it is" nor asserts "it is not. That which is like primordial non-existence is such that nothing is lost.
What they say is not frivolous; they do not speak of other matters but speak only of what is correct and balanced.
They do not observe or scrutinize the actions of others.
When one observes such characteristics and finds them fully endowed with such conduct, one knows that this is indeed an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does not assume the physical appearance or likeness of a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, thinking, 'This is a śramaṇa' or 'This is a brāhmaṇa.'"
Whatever he sees and knows, he understands it all as truth; he never performs sacrifices or prostrations to other devas, nor does he offer them flowers or incense.
Observing such characteristics and conduct in their entirety, one knows that this is indeed an *avaivartika* bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
An irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is never reborn in an evil realm, nor does he become a woman.
By thus examining his signs and conduct as they are fully possessed, one knows that this is indeed an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva never departs from the ten wholesome paths of action. He himself refrains from killing, and teaches others not to kill;

he himself refrains from stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech, frivolous speech, envy, greed for others' property, and malicious doubt; he personally practices what is right and teaches others to maintain what is right—these are the ten wholesome paths."

Furthermore, if in a dream one personally maintains the ten wholesome paths without loss, this is for an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva to personally see the ten wholesome paths face-to-face within a dream.
By observing their characteristics and conduct in this manner, one knows that they are indeed irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

The dharmas studied by the mind of an avaivartika bodhisattva-mahāsattva, which he maintains with the desire to bring peace and security to all people and for which he preaches the Dharma to them entirely—this is the gift of Dharma.
To cause all beings to attain the Dharma-realm is itself the giving of the Dharma to all.
Observing their characteristics and conduct in this manner, one knows that such a person is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! An avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva is like a king, a hero among men.

Possessing the wisdom known by his name, when he hears the teaching of the profound Dharma, he never harbors doubt. Having no doubt, he does not say he does not believe. His speech is gentle, his words are like honey. He sleeps little; whether entering or departing, walking or standing, his mind is undisturbed. He walks slowly and with steady steps, lifting his feet to tread upon the ground, choosing his path with care. Furthermore, his clothing contains no lice; he is constantly pure and clean, free from dust and grime, and without sorrow. Within his body, there are none of the eighty kinds of worms."
Why is this? Because all the merits of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas surpass even supramundane merits;
as they gradually seek to bring them to full completion, those merits increase manifold.
"His body is pure, and his mind is also pure.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha:
"How is this so, O God among Gods?"
“How can one know that the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is pure?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“The merit performed by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva increases manifold, becoming progressively more supreme; his mind is sovereign and unimpeded, for that merit is entirely attained by the mind and thus purified. It transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; this is called the purity of mind of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.”
Observing his characteristics and conduct in this manner, one knows that he is indeed an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva does not seek wealth;
if there are those who make offerings, he has no stinginess or greed; when teaching the profound Dharma, he never grows weary, but remains correctly established in knowledge."
To those who wish to hear the profound Dharma, one should uphold the Prajñāpāramitā and expound it for them.
For those who engage in other paths or worldly affairs, one should uphold the Prajñāpāramitā as the master to rectify them.
Those who do not understand, they shall cause to understand by means of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Observing their characteristics and conduct in this manner, one knows that these are indeed irreversible Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When [a bodhisattva] arrives, Māra the Evil One will come to that place and manifest eight great hells; in each hell, he will manifest hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas."
He then pointed them out and said:
"These people have all received their predictions from the Buddha and are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive).
Yet now they have all fallen into the hells."
All have received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha.
If one has already received the prediction of becoming an *avaivartika*, they should quickly repent, saying:
"I am not an *avaivartika*."
"If one were to say this, they would not enter hell but would instead be born in the heavens.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If the mind remains unmoved, such a person is an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva."
The Buddha said,
"What I have spoken is without error.
If one were to be born in an evil realm, then my words would be false."
By observing their signs and conduct in this manner, one knows that they are indeed irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
The evil Māra may transform himself into a śramaṇa, wearing the robes of one, and approach the bodhisattva mahāsattva, saying:
"Whatever you previously heard from me and whatever you received from me, you must now completely renounce; all of it is useless. You must now repent for your transgressions."
If you repent quickly and follow my words, I shall come every day in person to inquire after your well-being;
if you do not heed my words, I shall never come to see you again.
If you no longer say that these words were not spoken by the Buddha, but rather that they were all fabricated by other outsiders, then what I am now saying is indeed the word of the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One who wavers upon hearing this teaching should be known as a person who has not received the prediction (vyākaraṇa) from a past Buddha.
Among those present here among the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, there are many bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have not yet reached the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika)."
If one remains unshakable, one contemplates that dharmas are devoid of birth and death; one contemplates the absence of birth and death without relying on the words of others.
This is like a bhikṣu who has attained arhatship: he does not follow the words of others, but perceives all dharmas with his own eyes and takes them as direct realization.
This is because that which is non-existent can never be moved.

Likewise, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva cannot be moved; just as those who dwell on the stages of the path of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not turn back from the multitude of dharmas they have contemplated, so too this bodhisattva-mahāsattva, proceeding directly toward sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), cannot turn back.
By observing their characteristics and conduct through such comparisons, one knows that they are indeed irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
The evil Māra goes to where the bodhisattva mahāsattva is and transforms himself into another person, saying:
"That which you seek involves extreme hardship; it is not the practice of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)."
If one incurs this debt, for what purpose is this toil and suffering?
If one employs this toil and suffering, for what purpose?
Should one not grow weary of it as it is being performed?
"Where else could one seek such a body again?
Why did you not take arhatship earlier instead of seeking it for the sake of becoming a Buddha?
The Buddha said:
"If he does not waver or turn back, Māra the Evil One will again abandon him and devise another stratagem.
He will manifest as several bodhisattvas standing by his side and address him with a pointing finger, saying:
'Do you see these bodhisattvas? "

Having made offerings to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges, providing them all with robes, food, bedding, and medicine in full abundance; having practiced pure precepts in the presence of all those Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and having received their instructions and heard the wisdom therein, they shall act accordingly.
Regarding that which they seek—having studied it all thoroughly and abiding according to the Dharma—they are currently unable to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
