Having studied in this way, having accepted it in this way, and having practiced in this way, they cannot attain *sarvajñatā*; how much less so if they wish to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha said:
"If he remains unmoved, the evil Māra will depart.
He will then further transform himself into a bhikṣu and speak these words:"
"These are all arhats who, in past lives, all practiced the bodhisattva path, yet now have all attained arhatship.
If even these bhikṣus are currently like this, from what could they possibly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
The Buddha said:

"Although this bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears these words from another source, he continues to practice accordingly; his mind does not waver or shift, nor does he harbor any contrary thoughts, for he recognizes them as the work of Māra."
The Buddha said:
"If there were one who, while practicing the study of the *pāramitās*, could not attain *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), from what then could it be attained?
What the Buddha speaks is without any discrepancy."

If one trains in this way and practices in this way, with a mind that does not waver as it accords with the *prajñāpāramitā*, even if one does not thereby attain *sarvajñatā*, there would be a discrepancy in the Buddha’s words.
What the Buddha has spoken can never be deceptive; this is how a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should train.
By using these analogies to observe whether their marks and conduct are complete, one knows that they are indeed an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One approaches an irreversible bodhisattva and speaks to them thus:
'The state of omniscience (sarvajñatā) is like space; this dharma has no boundaries or limits, and this dharma cannot be found to have any ultimate attainment that can be grasped.'"
Why is this? Because there is no such thing as an avaivartika, nor is there anyone who attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
As I now contemplate these dharmas, they are entirely empty.
Whatever he does is merely toil and hardship; he should not perceive this as being the work of Māra.
How then can he hope to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
"This is not what was spoken by the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"These sons and daughters of good family should understand it thus; they should maintain this thought that it is the work of Māra, and their minds shall remain upright and unshakable."
By observing their characteristics and conduct through this comparison, one knows that they are indeed irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to enter the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third, up to the fourth dhyāna samāpatti, he follows these four dhyānas without recording them as specific dhyāna-objects; this is his samāpatti, because it is for the sake of others.
By observing their signs and conduct through this analogy, one knows that they are indeed irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
An avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva does not seek the praise of those who mention his name.
Even if his name is proclaimed, he does not harbor thoughts of desire; his mind is vast and expansive, thinking only of how to bring peace and security to all beings.

In walking, standing, sitting, and rising, his mind is not distracted; in his coming and going, he applies his attention with propriety and sincerity. He does not seek power, nor does he engage in illicit lust.
If he wishes to go or come, he regards his own desires as a source of affliction, and he is always filled with dread toward sensual desire.
It is like a man who, having passed through a vast wilderness, desires food and drink but fears robbers and bandits and wishes to depart in haste.
He thinks to himself:
"When shall I reach a secure village and quickly escape?"

The *avaivartika* bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: when moving through the realms of craving and existence, he reflects that what he has done is improper, that it is wrong, and that it is entirely incorrect; he considers it not to be the work of his own Dharma, nor does he harbor any other evil thoughts.
"Why is this? Because I wish to cause all beings to attain peace and security.
The Buddha said:
"Whatever thoughts they form, all are due to the majestic spiritual power of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
By observing their signs and conduct through such comparison and analysis, one knows that this is indeed an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, the yakṣa Vairambha constantly follows and attends upon the bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible (avaivartika). Other spirits and deities do not dare to associate with him; he never loses his resolve, his mind is not distracted, and his body does not act recklessly. His physical form is complete and without deficiency. He is a hero among men; he does not seduce the wives of others. Whether by means of talismans, incantations, or medicinal herbs, he never engages in such things himself, nor does he teach others to do so. This is the purity of a bodhisattva."
He does not speak of the affairs of men, nor does he speak of the affairs of women; he is entirely free from such faults.
By observing his characteristics and conduct through these comparisons, one knows that he is indeed an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

An *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva does not engage in affairs with crowds of people, nor with kings, nor with thieves, nor with weapons, nor with armies, nor with villages, nor with cities, nor with worldly matters, nor with women, nor with men, nor with other paths, nor with grain, nor with necessities, nor with sacrifices, nor with various colors, nor with flowers, nor with incense, nor with frivolous play. He does not follow after the sea, nor after profit, nor does he perform various kinds of [worldly] works; he does not engage in any affair whatsoever, but engages only in the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Not departing from omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they constantly maintain mindfulness without forgetting it, nor do they engage in conflict or worldly affairs.
They maintain themselves according to the Dharma, always practicing what is right and central, and never following what is contrary to the Dharma.

They constantly praise the worthy as supreme; they always desire to be intimate and friendly with others rather than harboring resentment or malice; they seek only the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and thus desire to be reborn in the Buddha-fields of other directions.

By making such a request, one will not be reborn in those realms; for this reason, one shall constantly behold the Buddhas and further obtain the opportunity to make offerings to the *avaivartika* bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Whether from the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm, they depart from those places and are reborn in a central land; they are born into the families of the virtuous, or among those who are wise, or into families where discourse is practiced, or into households that understand the scriptures, and they take no pleasure in trivial affairs.
Those who were born in border regions are all now born in great central lands and never violate the law.
By observing these signs and the perfection of their conduct through such comparisons, one knows that they are indeed irreversible Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not say:
'I am irreversible.'"
Nor does he think:
"I am an avaivartika," nor does he harbor any self-doubt.
"I am not on the stage of the avaivartika.
This is like a man who has attained the path of srotāpanna; he will never have any doubt regarding that stage of the path.
Although the works of Māra may arise, he perceives them all completely;
once they have arisen, he does not follow their schemes.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva of irreversible stage (*avaivartika*) is also like this: he never harbors doubt regarding his own level of the Path, nor does he ever become indolent.
Although the works of Māra arise, he perceives them all completely;
once they have arisen, he does not follow their schemes.
It is like a man who has committed a heinous crime; his mind never forgets it, and until the end of his life, his mind can never be turned away from it.

An Avaivartika Bodhisattva Mahāsattva can never be diverted; his mind is established in loyalty and rectitude, and within the state of an Avaivartika Bodhisattva, his mind can never be shaken, nor can he ever be turned back by anything in the heavens above or the earth below.
Although the works of Māra arise, he fully perceives them all;
once they have arisen, he does not follow their schemes.
He never harbors doubt regarding his own stage of the Path, nor does he possess the mind of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha.
He never thinks:
"The Buddha is difficult to encounter; his realm is peaceful and secure, firmly established, and unsurpassed. Why is this?
One who dwells in this manner cannot be surpassed.
Māra, the Evil One, became deeply distressed and, manifesting himself as a Buddha, went to that person's location and said:
"If you should gather the realization of an Arhat, the Tathāgata will grant you the prediction that you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Why is this? If one cannot attain comparison, one also cannot attain characteristics.

As for those whose minds engage in such comparisons, even if they are fully endowed with these characteristics and practices, they may still fail to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi as Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"How could he possibly attain it?
The Buddha said,

"If the mind of this bodhisattva-mahāsattva remains unshaken and unwavering, one should know that this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has already received the prediction of enlightenment from the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
Furthermore, if one should think thus:
"I know that this man has come in the form of a Buddha created by Māra; he is not a Buddha, but this is the work of Māra.
To act in such a way so as to correspond to the stage of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva is no different from the deeds of Māra as described by the Buddha.
"If he observes thus and reflects thus, he will know that these are the deeds of Māra, intended to cause him to turn back.
The Buddha said, "If he remains unmoved,
this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has received his prediction from the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and dwells already in the stage of Avaivartika."
Why is this? By using these comparisons to observe the fulfillment of his marks and conduct, one knows that he is indeed an *avaivartika*.
Thus, by comparing and observing the fulfillment of his marks and conduct, one knows that he is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is truly *avaivartika*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva relies upon the Dharma, he does not covet anything that belongs to him, nor does he cherish his own body or life."
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva desires to fully receive the Dharma in order to protect all the teachings of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
To desire to protect the Buddha-Dharma of the past, future, and present and thereby be counted among the ranks of the Sangha—this is the definitive resolve; this is the protection of the Dharma.
For this reason, he has nothing for which he feels attachment; he does not even begrudge his life or body, never becoming weary at any time and never experiencing exhaustion.
By observing such characteristics and conduct in their full measure, one knows that this is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
regarding the Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, an Avaivartika Bodhisattva Mahāsattva never entertains doubt, nor does he say it is not so."
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"Regarding the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, one neither doubts it nor speaks of it as being wrong.
When he teaches the Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas, does one likewise neither doubt it nor speak of it as being wrong?"
"Whatever Dharma the śrāvakas teach, one neither doubts it nor says it is wrong.
Why is this, Subhūti? "
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva has attained the patient acceptance of the joy in the dharma of non-arising.
By means of this comparative observation of his characteristics and conduct being fully complete, one knows him to be an irreversible bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Chapter Nine: The Laywoman Viśākhā. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How great! Are the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are *avaivartika*!"
From great merit, one attains for oneself the stage of *avaivartika*; this is accomplished through practices as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Now, the God among Gods preaches the profound Dharma, which is the practice performed by these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"

That which you have internalized is profound; it is emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the absence of birth and death, the absence of arising, the absence of existence, and the absence of desire—it is cessation.
"Nirvāṇa is that which constitutes a limit.
Subhūti said to the Buddha, "Nirvāṇa is a limit; it is not among all dharmas."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“All dharmas are profoundly deep. Why is this?
“Form, Subhūti, is profound;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also profound. The aggregates are as profound as form is profound.”
"What, Subhūti, is meant by the profound depth of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
That which is profound is not the profundity of form; rather, it is the profundity of form."
"It is the same with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; this consciousness is profoundly deep.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "How great!"
The subtle and wondrous form gradually conforms to nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness gradually conform to the profound depth of nirvāṇa; that which is profoundly deep is the Prajñāpāramitā.”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates and reflects in this way, this constitutes abiding.

Training in the perfection of wisdom according to the instructions of the *prajñāpāramitā*, this bodhisattva mahāsattva follows these reflections and contemplations; as taught regarding emptiness, they should practice for even a single day, which is profoundly deep and beyond words.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices for even a single day, how many kalpas of birth and death does this eliminate?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Suppose, Subhūti, there were a lustful man who deeply loved a beautiful woman and had made an appointment to meet her,
yet the woman was not at her own disposal. What do you think?”
"Does that man think of her?
Subhūti replied, "Because of the woman, he thinks of her very much; there is no time when he does not remember her."
The Buddha said:

"If a man’s thoughts remain thus for a single day without wavering, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, by contemplating the prajñāpāramitā, should practice it for one day; he will thereby eliminate the cycle of birth and death for many kalpas."

If one studies according to the teachings of the Prajñāpāramitā as explained therein, and practices them with mindfulness for even a single day, that bodhisattva has already repelled evil and eliminated transgressions.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva were separated from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), even if they were to practice giving for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, it would not equal a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who practices in accordance with the teachings of the perfection of wisdom for a single day; the latter's merit surpasses the former.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva were to live for as many eons as there are grains of sand on the banks of the Ganges, making offerings and giving gifts, yet bestowing them upon srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas while remaining apart from the prajñāpāramitā."

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who follows the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, their merit surpasses that of a bodhisattva who practices giving and maintains the precepts for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand on the banks of the Ganges.
If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, mindful of the prajñāpāramitā, gives rise to it and immediately preaches the Dharma, his merit will surpass that of the former bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by means of the gift of Dharma, increases his merit even further.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the gift of Dharma, this constitutes the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the gift of Dharma but does not maintain the Middle Way, their merit is not equal to that of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the gift of Dharma while maintaining the Middle Way.
"If there are those who uphold the Prajñāpāramitā and do not depart from guarding the Middle Way, the merit of these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is exceedingly great.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha:
"All things are without birth-and-death; if there is nothing that moves,"
“O God among Gods!
Of these two matters, which one possesses the greater merit?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, within the cycle of birth and death of merit and within the cycle of birth and death of virtue, practice the prajñāpāramitā with delight in emptiness, delight in non-existence, delight in cessation, and delight in non-apprehension.”
When one maintains this mindfulness, one is not separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one is not separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*, that bodhisattva mahāsattva attains incalculable, asankhyeya merits.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha:
"O God among Gods, what is meant by 'incalculable, asaṃkhyeya merit'?
What is its distinctive excellence?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Asaṃkhyeya means that its number cannot be exhausted.
‘Incalculable’ means it cannot be measured or calculated; its limits are utterly unattainable.”
"Therefore, they are incalculable *asaṃkhyeya*. Subhūti said:

"When the Buddha speaks of the 'incalculable,' form (*rūpa*) is also incalculable; feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are also incalculable."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"As you have said, form (rūpa) is also incalculable; feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) are also incalculable."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is meant by 'incalculable'?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Because it is like space, it is incalculable; because it is signless and wishless, it is said to be incalculable.
That which is thus incalculable is itself emptiness, and there is no other dharma apart from it."
The Buddha said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Do I not say that all dharmas are entirely empty?"
Subhūti said: "So it is, O God among Gods; all dharmas spoken by you are entirely empty and inexhaustible.
The Buddha said:
"In this way, Subhūti, all dharmas are entirely empty and incalculable;

there is no dharma that is distinct from another, nor can any differentiation, distinction, attainment, or non-attainment be found. This is precisely what the Tathāgata has attained: it is inexhaustible and incalculable, like emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the absence of birth-and-death, the absence of arising, the absence of existence, the absence of origination, and the absence of cessation—like nirvāṇa. According to what is preferred and according to what is taught, this is the teaching of the Tathāgata."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha: “How great!
The Dharma taught by the God among Gods is truly unattainable.”
"As I have spoken regarding the recollection of the Buddha, so too are all dharmas unattainable.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"In this way, all dharmas are entirely unattainable; because dharmas are like space, they are unattainable."
Subhūti said: “As the Buddha has taught that the fundamental is unattainable,
I pray that you explain this unattainability.”
The Buddha said, "No. Subhūti said:
“The six pāramitās are unattainable; this constitutes giving without increase or decrease.
The śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā are likewise without increase or decrease.”
This is precisely the six pāramitās, neither increasing nor decreasing.
What is meant by the six pāramitās being neither increasing nor decreasing?
This is how a bodhisattva-mahāsattva personally attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For what reason does he sit near the Buddha?
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from the *prajñāpāramitā*, thereby personally attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Just as that which is fundamentally unattainable neither increases nor decreases, so too the bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* with *upāyakauśalya* does not conceive of this as an increase or decrease of the *dānapāramitā*. He understands that this *prajñāpāramitā* is merely a name, and that this *dānapāramitā* consists of giving away all that one possesses.”
One should mentally take hold of these merits and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When such dedication is in accord with *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
To practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way is what constitutes *upāyakauśalya*.

One does not dwell upon the increase or decrease of the *śīlapāramitā*, but regards it merely as a name; this is the *śīlapāramitā*, and this is the mental attention of the mind of ethical discipline (*śīlacitta*). To dedicate these merits toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and to give as if giving toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—this is for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva to be practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The same applies to the *kṣānti-pāramitā*, *vīrya*, and *dhyāna-pāramitā*.

For this bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the *prajñā-pāramitā* with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they do not conceive of the increase or decrease of the *prajñā-pāramitā*; it is merely a name.

To practice the *prajñāpāramitā* is to give rise to the mind of wisdom; to take these merits and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, dedicating them as if they were *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* itself—this is what constitutes true giving.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the gift of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"That which is fundamentally non-existent is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is neither increasing nor decreasing.
Constantly following this mindfulness, one never departs from its practice and is now close to sitting upon the seat of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Thus it is, Subhūti!
That which is fundamentally non-existent cannot be attained, nor does it increase or decrease.
To contemplate and reflect upon this is to have nothing lost; this is the perfection that does not diminish.
"If this bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates and dwells upon these thoughts, he will distance himself from the seat of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintains his mind at the moment of first generating the resolve, he should draw near to the seat of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
If one maintains the final thought-moment, one draws near to the seat of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
There is no opposition between the initial thought-moment and the final thought-moment;
likewise, there is no opposition between the final thought-moment and the initial thought-moment.
"By what kind of merit are they produced?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"For example, when a lamp wick is burning, does that wick burn by means of the initial light?"
"Can it be ignited by means of the later flame? Subhūti replied,
"It is neither ignited by means of the initial flame, nor is it ignited apart from the initial flame."
"Nor does it burn by means of the subsequent light, nor does it burn apart from the subsequent light.
The Buddha said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
"Is it so? Subhūti replied, "So it is, so it is!"
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the initial mind, nor does he attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi apart from the initial mind."
“Nor does one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of a subsequent mind, nor does one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* apart from a subsequent mind.
Subhūti said to the Buddha,
“The causal conditions are profound.”
O God among Gods!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the initial mind, nor does he attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi apart from the initial mind;
nor does he attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the final mind, nor does he attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi apart from the final mind.
“Subhūti, how is it? Does the preceding mind cease,
and does the subsequent mind arise?”
Subhūti said: “No, O God among Gods!”
“Subhūti, how is it? Does that mind which has first arisen cease?
Subhūti replied:
"That dharma is a dharma of cessation,
O God among Gods! How so, Subhūti?"
"Regarding that dharma which is to be extinguished,
can it indeed be extinguished? Subhūti replied, "No."
"O God among Gods!
Subhūti, how is it? Is it possible to abide in suchness as it originally is?"
Subhūti said: "Those who wish to abide should do so as being fundamentally non-existent.
[The Buddha asked: "How so, Subhūti?"
"Suppose it were to abide as it originally was,
would there not then be no difference? Subhūti replied, "No."
"O God among Gods!
Subhūti, how is it? Is that which is fundamentally non-existent profound?"
Subhūti said: “It is profound,
O God among Gods!”
“Subhūti, how is it? Is there a mind that is fundamentally unconditioned?
He replied:
“There is none,
O God among Gods! “How so, Subhūti?”
"Is there anyone who can have a different mind that was previously non-existent? He replied, "No."
"O God among Gods!
Subhūti, how is it? Do you not have the intention of seeing that which is fundamentally non-existent?"
He replied:
“No, O God among Gods.”
“Subhūti, how is it? Is one who practices in this way practicing the profound?
He replied:
“O God among Gods! To perform such an action is to perform no action at all.
Why is this? Because...”
"Acting thus is non-seeing action; it is the practice of the invisible.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, what is it that they practice?"
Subhūti said: "He practices with thorough discernment,
O God among Gods!"
“Subhūti, how is it? Does one who practices the truths practice with conceptualization?
He replied:
"No, O God among Gods! Why is that, Subhūti?"
“Does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva give rise to the conceptualization of consciousness? He replied, “No.”
"O God among Gods!
Subhūti, how is it? Is it that one does not cognize the perception, yet it is still a perception?"
Subhūti said: “A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not act in this way. [The Buddha asked: “How so, Subhūti?”
“Without forming conceptualizations, one attains that which should be practiced and fulfills all Buddha-dharmas;

is this not the path of a bodhisattva, rather than that of a śrāvaka? Subhūti replied, “The bodhisattva-mahāsattva who possesses *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) has no craving for even the state of non-conceptualization.”
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while dreaming, enters the three samādhis and contemplates the gate of liberation of emptiness-of-emptiness, signlessness-of-signlessness, and wishlessness-of-wishlessness, is this samādhi beneficial?"
The Prajñāpāramitā is beneficial during the day and night;
it is likewise beneficial even during dreams at night. Why is this?
"What the Buddha has taught is that whether it be during the day or within a night dream, they are equal and no different.
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the *prajñāpāramitā* during the day, he likewise contemplates the *prajñāpāramitā* with even greater intensity within a dream at night."
Śāriputra said: "How is it, Subhūti?
If something is done in a dream, does it truly exist?"
He replied: "No.
The teaching of all dharmas is also like that which exists within a dream."
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
“If one performs wholesome deeds in a dream and feels great joy upon waking, this constitutes an increase.
If one commits unwholesome deeds and does not feel remorse, this constitutes a decrease.”
Śāriputra said:
"Suppose one commits a killing within a dream and feels great joy in one's heart;
having awakened, one says:"
"I have killed this one; how great is my joy!
What does this mean? Subhūti said:
"It is not false; all have causes and conditions.
The mind does not exist in vain; it must have an object of perception.
Whether seen, heard, or thought, one becomes aware and knows it. Because of these causes and conditions, the human mind becomes attached, and thus there is that which is acquired."
What is meant by "that which is obtained"?
One undergoes retribution based on causes and conditions; one does not undergo retribution without causes and conditions, for all things arise from causes and conditions.
Śāriputra said:
"All that is produced through causes and conditions is merely illusory and entirely empty.
World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions is [the Tathāgata] born?"
He replied,
"It arises conditioned by perception.
Śāriputra said:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving in a dream and, taking this gift, dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
does that constitute a gift or not?"
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"The Great Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya is currently near here; in a few days, he shall succeed to the position of the Buddha."
"Whoever has a question may ask it, and I shall immediately provide an answer.
Śāriputra said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"Regarding what I have just asked, Subhūti said:"
“Mahā-Maitreya Bodhisattva will be able to explain it.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Śāriputra:

“As my name is Maitreya, that which I shall explain must be explained by means of form (rūpa), or it must be explained by means of feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna).”

Form is itself emptiness; one should understand this through non-existence. If one understands that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, and does not perceive even the dharma that is to be understood, what understanding could there be?
"Furthermore, one does not perceive any dharma that is to be understood as 'one shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"What you have spoken is already realized."
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Śāriputra:
"The Dharma that is taught does not speak of attaining realization.
Thereupon, Śāriputra had this thought:
“The wisdom entered by Maitreya Bodhisattva is exceedingly profound.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā has existed for a very long time.”
The Buddha said,
"What do you think, Śāriputra?
Can one truly perceive that person as being an arhat?"
Śāriputra said: “No, O God among Gods!”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“It is likewise for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā; he does not think:
‘I shall receive the prediction of enlightenment from this dharma.’”
"One does not attain certainty through these dharmas.

If, through these dharmas, one is to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and personally realize *abhisambuddha*, then this bodhisattva mahāsattva acts in such a way and practices the *prajñāpāramitā* that he has no fear of not attaining *abhisambuddha*.
One who follows this teaching practices the *prajñāpāramitā*.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva acts with fearlessness. Why is this?
If one arrives at a place of extreme peril amidst tigers and wolves, neither fearing nor being terrified, one thinks in the mind:
"Should anyone devour me, I shall offer it as a gift."
This constitutes the fulfillment of the practice of the dānapāramitā and brings one close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
May I become a Buddha and cause that buddha-field to be free from the paths of birds and beasts.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva encounters a great band of fierce robbers, they feel no fear or dread. Why is this?
Even if they were to die therein, they would think to themselves:
"My body shall inevitably be cast aside; even if someone were to kill me, I would feel no anger.
This is the fulfillment of the practice of patience, the pāramitā of kṣānti, by which one shall draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"May it be that when I become a Buddha, there shall be no thieves or robbers among the people of my land.
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reaches a place where there is no water or drink, he is not afraid or terrified, and thinks to himself:
"All people think that I have no merit, which has caused this lack of water and drink."
"I vow that when I become a Buddha, there shall always be water of eight flavors within my land, so that all people may fully utilize it.
For the sake of worldly beings, he constantly exerts himself with diligence.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva reaches a place where grain is scarce, he feels no fear or dread, thinking to himself:

"I shall firm up my diligence so that I may personally attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; when I have realized unexcelled perfect enlightenment, there shall be no evil in my buddha-field, and all people therein shall have whatever food and drink they desire appear before them, just as it is in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
For the sake of all people, this good man applies himself with diligence until he personally attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieves *abhisambuddha*.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is in the midst of evil bandits, they are likewise not afraid or terrified.
Why is this? Because they do not perceive any phenomenon that could cause them pain.
For this reason, he has no fear:
"Even if my own body were to encounter such illness and death, my mind would remain unchanged, and I would surely continue with diligent effort.
I vow that when I attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and become a Buddha, there shall be no one in that buddha-field who is defiled by evil or who dies."
"What this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has spoken is no different from the words of the Buddha.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva will before long attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; having personally realized unexcelled perfect enlightenment, he shall likewise feel no fear regarding his own dharma."
Why is this? From the beginningless limit (*anādikoti*) until now, it has not been long since he first resolved his mind [on enlightenment].
How many such beginningless limits are there?
Is it for a long time? Is it for an exceedingly long time?
A single mental moment is the ultimate limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are now close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and will attain *abhisambodhi*, they hear this now and are not terrified.
At that time, the upāsikā rose from her seat, went forward to pay homage to the Buddha, knelt on her right knee, and addressed the Buddha:
“Having heard these words, I am neither afraid nor terrified; I shall certainly later preach the Dharma for all people so that they may not be afraid or terrified.”
At that moment, the Buddha smiled, and five-colored light issued from his mouth.
When the smile had ended,
the upāsikā took golden flowers and scattered them over the Buddha.
By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, those flowers remained above the Buddha and did not fall to the ground.
Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, stepped forward to pay homage to the Buddha, and then knelt with his right knee on the ground to ask the Buddha:
"The smile of the Tathāgata is never without cause; there must surely be something he intends to say."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"This laywoman Gaṅgādhārā, in a future age, during a kalpa named Nakṣatra, shall become a buddha; his title shall be Suvarṇapuṣpa Buddha."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"This upāsikā shall hereafter cast off her female form, receive a male body, and be reborn in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha."
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra-sūtra, Scroll Four;
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra-sūtra, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmapriya and Zhu Fonian during the Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Ten: Abiding in Emptiness Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what way does one who abides in emptiness practice non-attachment?”
“What is meant by ‘guarding emptiness’ being itself samādhi?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā contemplates the emptiness of form, and contemplates the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
"One who practices this contemplation is single-minded.
Just as in what is contemplated, one sees nothing in phenomena, nor does one realize anything within phenomena.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What the Buddha has taught is that one does not realize emptiness through meditative attainment.
How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not realize emptiness through samādhi?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“This bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that all forms whatsoever are empty, yet does not realize this as a final attainment.
One who practices such contemplation does not grasp at realization; by not realizing through contemplation, one is free from craving.”
This is contemplation; because there is nothing to crave, this is itself contemplation.
When one is about to enter [this state] but does not yet realize non-craving, at that time the mind does not dwell on the causal conditions of samādhi—this is mindfulness.
At that time, in order not to lose the Bodhisattva’s fundamental dharma and not to attain realization midway, why is this?
Because the dharmas of the meritorious deeds performed are extremely profound; since one does not crave such moments, one does not take realization.
They obtain protection by following the Prajñāpāramitā.

It is, for example, like a person who is brave or resilient and capable of repelling enemies; such a person is upright and powerful, there is nothing they cannot do, they fully understand the sixty-four variations of military strategy, they have mastered the five types of knowledge, and they are revered by the multitude.
In every place he goes, there is no benefit he does not obtain; what he thus acquires he distributes further to others, so that both he and the people are without exception filled with joy.

If there should be some other matter such that he must pass through great and extreme peril together with his parents, wife, and children, the person will then bring peace to his parents, wife, and children, saying:
"Do not fear, do not be terrified; we shall now all emerge from this peril together."

If, while they are there, an enemy should suddenly arrive, that person, being wise and alert, would immediately have his parents, wife, and children escort him back to his native village; everyone would return safe and sound without harm, and the enemy likewise would suffer no injury.
Why is this? Because there is nothing he does not understand; that person is courageous and capable of transformations, surpassing his enemies.
Whenever his enemies see him, they are all struck with terror and flee away.
When their parents, wives, and children emerge from the midst of the calamity and return to their homes, there is none who does not rejoice.
In this same way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses a mind of supreme great compassion toward all people.

At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, maintaining a mind of loving-kindness, bestows everything upon others; he transcends all turbid defilements and the domains of Māra, and further emerges above the stages of the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The bodhisattva abides within samādhi without exhaustion; by means of the pāramitās, they are without craving for emptiness.

When practicing in this way, this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the samādhi of emptiness directed toward the gates of liberation, yet neither by means of signs nor by means of signlessness, and thus does not realize [nirvana] prematurely.
Subhūti, it is like a flying bird that soars through the air without encountering any obstruction.

In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice emptiness to reach emptiness, proceed toward signlessness to reach signlessness, and proceed toward wishlessness to reach wishlessness; yet they do not fall away because of emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness, for they desire to fully perfect all the dharmas of a Buddha.
Subhūti, it is like a skilled archer who shoots into the air;

as the arrow remains suspended in the sky, he shoots another arrow that strikes the first one, and continues to shoot subsequent arrows, each hitting the preceding one so that none fall to the ground. Only when that person wishes for the first arrow to fall does it finally fall.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* is sustained by *upāyakauśalya*; they do not realize the truth midway through the limit of the beginning (*pūrvakoṭi*), but fulfill their merits and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having fulfilled these merits, they become Buddhas and are able to bear witness to the limit of the beginning.
"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom; this dharma gives rise to dharma.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva truly undergoes the hardship of such training, yet does not realize the fruit midway."
"How great!
O God among Gods, from his original practice he has been secure and at ease, and has by himself attained Buddhahood.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva desires to protect all people, and because this is brought about by his original vow, he is able to protect all beings and bring them to liberation; this is the mental discernment directed toward the gate of liberation through the samādhi of guarding emptiness."
What is meant by "discrimination"?

It is the discrimination of the samādhi of emptiness, the discrimination of the samādhi of signlessness, and the discrimination of the samādhi of wishlessness; yet one does not realize the ultimate limit midway.
Why is this? Because they are protected by *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means); at the time of first generating the mind of enlightenment, they resolve to protect all beings.
Maintaining this resolve, they enter into *upāyakauśalya*, and therefore do not realize [nirvana] midway.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva has deeply entered the state of liberation, they [enter] the emptiness samādhi as a gate of liberation, the signlessness samādhi as a gate of liberation, and the wishlessness samādhi as a gate of liberation."
For this reason, his mind makes such distinctions. This person has come from a long time ago;

by means of the practices he has undertaken, he causes those very causes to be abandoned. This is the teaching of the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is the guarding of the *śūnyatā-samādhi* directed toward liberation, the guarding of the *animitta-samādhi* directed toward liberation, and the guarding of the *apraṇihita-samādhi* directed toward liberation. This is the *apraṇihita-samādhi* directed toward liberation, wherein the original mind that was aroused is endowed with *upāya-kauśalya*, so that one does not realize the ultimate limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) midway. This is being undiminished in compassion; this is the *maitrī-samādhi* and the *karuṇā-samādhi*.
Why is this? It is because of their skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva, for the sake of benefiting the Dharma, attains manifold wisdom, accomplishes the powers, and there is nothing they do not realize.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

That which is contemplated by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is this: that person has, for a long time past, been beneficial to the Dharma; they have attained what is to be known, perfected their powers, and there is nothing they do not awaken to."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, this is what a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates: he knows that from long ago, people have possessed perceptions and consciousness, and thus they call it 'self'."

When attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for the sake of all people, he preaches the Dharma to them, causing them to give rise to the thought of awakening and enter the gate of liberation through the signless samādhi.
This is *upāyakauśalya*. For this reason, one does not realize the limit of reality midway;

this is non-diminution regarding loving-kindness, this is the *rakṣā-samapraticchanda-samādhi*, and this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva benefits the Dharma, attains what is to be known, perfects their power, and there is nothing they do not awaken to.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This is what a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates: he contemplates that for people since time immemorial, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, and the perception of emptiness have been present."
The Bodhisattva thinks to himself:
"When I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for the sake of all people, I shall preach the Dharma to them."
"Impermanence arises from pleasure; emptiness arises from existence; and non-self arises from self.
By means of this reflection, one attains *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means); this is the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Knowing that the Buddha does not sit in samādhi through samādhi, but desires only to fulfill all the dharmas of a Buddha, this is the gate of liberation of wishlessness (apraṇihita) without realizing it.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand this: regarding that which is the arousal of the mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, as for the person who has so aroused it, from long ago they have practiced without anything to practice; they do not conceptualize while practicing within conceptualization; they seek without practicing conceptualization within conceptualization; they do not practice the accumulation of conceptualization within the accumulation of conceptualization; they do not practice "possessing" within what is possessed by their practice; and they do not practice "impropriety" within what is improper in their practice.
He reflects so as to cause all persons to be non-existent.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects in this way, he does so by means of clarity regarding all persons.
When he forms this reflection, it constitutes *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means); it constitutes a profound and subtle contemplation of those dharmas.
That which is emptiness is itself signlessness and wishlessness; this is the absence of birth-and-death, which is itself the absence of that which is born and the absence of anything existing.
Subhūti, this is the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Since dharmas are unarisen, one does not perceive them within the triple world; thus, when someone comes to ask a question, [the bodhisattva] responds accordingly.
Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva desires to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for this reason he wishes to know that dharma.
How should he give rise to the mind of rare treasure?

For a bodhisattva mahāsattva, one does not realize emptiness, nor signlessness, nor wishlessness; one does not realize saṃsāra, nor anything that arises, nor does one realize through non-attention—this is called recollecting the prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti, this is the case:

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has already received the prediction of enlightenment contemplates as empty, signless, wishless, without birth and death, and without origin; he contemplates as non-existent, its very root being non-being.
Those who do not give rise to a wholesome mind cannot understand this.
Those who are able to comprehend it are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have heard of the matter of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from past Buddhas.
Since their minds do not waver,
for what reason is it that there are further bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, though mindful of the Dharma, are unable to clarify it?
"If there are those who question them, they are likewise unable to resolve or explain [the matter].
This is because they have not yet entered the stage of the bodhisattva path; they do not belong within the realm of the *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive).
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“If one does not hear what is spoken in the *pāramitās*, yet those who do hear it and those who do not hear it are both able to understand its wisdom, such a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is *avaivartika*.”
Subhūti said: “O God among Gods, there are very many who are bodhisattvas,
but few are able to understand.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"There are few bodhisattvas who abide in the stage of the wisdom of *avaivartika*; only those who have received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) are able to understand this.
The merit of such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is exceedingly great; it is not something known by the worlds of devas, humans, or asuras."
11. Chapter on Detachment: "Furthermore, Subhūti, as for that which is the truth:

a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even in a dream, does not enter the stage of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; he does not think of anything to be sought within the three realms, nor does he seek anything therein. He views all dharmas as like a dream and does not realize [enlightenment] therein."
Subhūti, you should know that this is the mark of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti:

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in a dream, assembles with several hundreds, several thousands, or several billions of disciples, he sits therein and preaches the Dharma to the community of bhikṣus, just as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha preaches the Dharma.
Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible;
you should know that these are the marks of one who is irreversible.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva flies into the air while in a dream and sits there to preach the Dharma to the community of bhikṣus, he sees for himself a radiance seven feet high. He manifests transformations at will in other places, and his deeds are just like the Dharma taught by a Buddha."
One who sees this in a dream should know that this is a mark of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is in a dream, they feel no fear, no dread, no anxiety, and no terror. Even if they see a district or commandery where armies have risen up and are attacking one another in succession; or if a fire breaks out; or if they see tigers, wolves, lions, and other beasts; or if they see someone cutting off human heads; or if they witness other such transformations involving extreme suffering and great destitution, such as those who are hungry and thirsty facing such calamities—their minds remain without fear, without dread, without alarm, and without wavering.
Whatever one sees in a dream during the night, upon awakening one immediately rises from one's seat and reflects thus:
"All that exists in the world is like a dream.
When I become a Buddha, I shall preach the Dharma for them all and instruct them everywhere."
"You should know that these are the marks of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
how is it known that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
When he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there shall be no evil whatsoever within his realm.
Subhūti, it is precisely this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who,
even in a dream, [sees] animals preying upon one another or the people suffering from epidemics.
His mind gradually forms this thought:
"May it be that when I become a Buddha, there shall be no evil whatsoever within my realm.
For this reason, one knows that his marks are pure; one should know that these are the marks of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens from a dream and sees a calamitous fire of evil arise, he forms this thought:
'What I have seen in my dream is no different from [the state of] equanimity of mind.'"
"By maintaining these analogies and being endowed with these marks, one knows that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is *avaivartika*. Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
'If I am truly one who practices according to the marks, then it shall be exactly as I have said, without any difference.'"
"Now, as for this fire that has broken out within the city walls, it shall be completely extinguished and vanish so that it is no longer seen.
The Buddha said:

"If the fire is entirely extinguished and vanishes, know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has received a prediction; he has received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from a past Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and know him to be an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive)."
If the fire does not go out but is extinguished [by his will], know that this bodhisattva has not yet received the prediction (vyākaraṇa).
Suppose the fire burns down one house and leaves another;
it then leaps across to burn one *li* and leaves another *li*.
It is so, Subhūti!
You should know that this was caused by the sin of obstructing the Dharma committed by these householders in their previous lives.
To realize that the deeds of such people are all the result of past karma—this is what is meant by "past destiny."
One should reflect so as to eliminate all the evils encountered in the present life.
By means of this, the karmic retribution of those dharmas that have been severed will be entirely extinguished.
For this reason, Subhūti!
"You should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is indeed irreversible from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, Subhūti,"
By means of these corresponding signs, one should recognize that his practice is complete; one should regard this bodhisattva mahāsattva as an avaivartika.
For this reason, I speak of these corresponding signs and practices so that they may be known.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
if at any time a man or woman is possessed by or seized by a spirit,
that bodhisattva might think:

"If I have received this prediction, and if the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas have indeed conferred upon me the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then even though my present suffering is truly different [from that of others], I shall surely attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and become a Samyaksaṃbuddha."
If one’s thoughts regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment are entirely pure, this serves to eliminate the mind of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha.
If one were to set aside the minds of arhats and pratyekabuddhas, one would inevitably attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; one cannot fail to achieve it and realize self-attained *abhisaṃbodhi*.
If one shall attain Buddhahood as an Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there are no Buddhas currently residing in incalculable lands who do not see them, and none who do not certify their realization.

Now the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha fully knows my thoughts without error; if I truly shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and become a Buddha, and if it is indeed as I have spoken, then this spirit-demon shall depart immediately.
He then asked,
"By which spirit or deity is this man or woman possessed?
Upon hearing his words, the spirit immediately departed.

When these words were spoken, if one does not depart, that bodhisattva has not yet received the prediction; the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past have not conferred upon him the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If, upon these words being spoken, Māra immediately departs, one should know that this bodhisattva has received a prediction; he has been granted the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If that person is truly sincere, Māra the Evil One will go to where the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells.
Then, if the bodhisattva says:"
"If I am truly sincere and have already received the prediction of attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then these evil spirits and ghosts shall depart immediately.
Because the wicked Māra acted thus with a virtuous mind, he transformed them so that all the evil spirits and ghosts departed.
Why is this? Because Māra is most exalted and possesses awesome spiritual power, none of the various malevolent ghosts and spirits dare to confront him;
all of these are warded off by the awesome spiritual power of Māra.
For this reason, they are all completely eliminated.
If a bodhisattva thinks to themselves:
"It is by virtue of my own majestic spiritual power."
Because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consider themselves thus, they instead become conceited; they treat others with contempt, mock them, and show no regard for them.
He says to others:
"I have received the prediction of enlightenment from the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, whereas all these other people have not yet received their predictions."

They have been granted the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by the Buddha; as for all other people, they have not yet received the prediction for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete bodhi.

Because of this, they become self-important and arrogant, their anger gradually increases, and they immediately distance themselves far from *sarvajñatā*, losing the wisdom of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Knowing that these bodhisattvas lack *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) and are thus arrogant, they fall into the two paths, the stage of the śrāvaka or the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
"Subhūti, these bodhisattvas take what is unaccomplished as accomplished;
they do not recognize the work of Māra, yet instead abandon their good teachers and depart, neither associating with them nor regarding them with respect."
For this reason, they are beset by Māra.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize that this is the work of Māra.
How does one discern it?
He perceives that a Māra has come before the bodhisattva; the Māra manifests transformations, appearing in various garbs as he comes and goes, and speaks these words:

"If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha of the past, [the Buddha] may know: his original surname was such-and-such; his mother’s name was such-and-such; his father’s name was such-and-such; his elder brother’s name was such-and-such; his elder sister’s name was such-and-such; his younger brother’s name was such-and-such; the name of his close friend was such-and-such; the name of his paternal uncle was such-and-such; the name of his seventh-generation paternal grandfather was such-and-such; the name of his maternal family was such-and-such; the name of his paternal family was such-and-such; he was born in such-and-such city, or born in such-and-such country, or born in such-and-such commandery, or born in such-and-such district, or born in such-and-such village."
"If one always speaks with gentle words, or causes others to speak such words, it is all brought about by what was done in previous lives, and thus one likewise speaks with gentle words.
At other times, those of high talent will further speak according to their own nature:
"In previous lives as well, I was likewise eminent and brilliant."

Some were seen maintaining self-restraint; some were seen begging for food; some ate at a single location, while others went directly to where food was offered; some first ate fruits and vegetables before eating rice, while others did otherwise; some stayed among burial mounds, some in secluded places, and some dwelt among the trees; some accepted invitations, while others did not; some took only as much as was sufficient, while others stayed in one place; some did not anoint their bodies with sesame oil, some had pleasant voices, and some engaged in conversation with one another.
Why is this? Māra spoke again:
"These causes and conditions are all brought about by the merit of former lives, which has enabled one to attain this."

‘If in a previous life he was the son of such-and-such a family, or of the Kṣatriya caste, or had such-and-such a name, and possessed such virtues in his previous life, then for that reason he is likewise so now.
That Bodhisattva then forms this thought and perception:
‘I am just like him.’”
Then that evil Māra spoke again, saying:
"If you have received this prediction, it is because the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas conferred upon you the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"By virtue of these causes and conditions and this merit, he must be an *avaivartika* [non-retrogressive] Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"It is not as I have described regarding the *avaivartika* Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."

If one examines by means of these comparative signs and conducts, and does not attain what I have described in its fullness, but instead acts according to one's own whims, you should know that such bodhisattvas will ultimately fail and be ruined by Māra.
Why is this? By using such comparisons to observe their characteristics and conduct, one knows that they are not indeed *avaivartika* [non-retrogressive] bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva never possesses such thoughts.

When these bodhisattvas hear the names mentioned by Māra, their hearts are filled with great joy; they believe it to be certain and consequently become arrogant, laughing at others in their conduct and treating their fellow students with contempt while acting only according to their own will.
"Subhūti, it is because that bodhisattva mahāsattva clings to this designation that he loses his fundamental essence and falls into the net of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti,"
Because they grasp at the word "receiving," these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not recognize it as the work of Māra; instead, they falsely claim to have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Māra then speaks further, saying:
"When you attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, when you become a Buddha, your name shall be such-and-such."
Upon hearing these words, the bodhisattva thinks to himself:
"It cannot be that I shall not attain it; for previously, I too have thought in this very same way."
The Buddha said:

"This bodhisattva possesses very little knowledge and lacks *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means). Instead, they harbor such thoughts and hope for a name, thinking: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and my title shall be such-and-such.'"
The Buddha said:
"Those who follow what Māra teaches proceed from the realm of Māra.
Now, these bhikṣus have been deluded by Māra; they think to themselves:"
"This is the result of my original aspiration; thus have I now obtained this name.
It is as it was said:
'In the past, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha bestowed upon me the prediction that I would attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Regarding those whom I have described as irreversible bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they do not act according to these signs, marks, and practices that I have used for comparison. Yet, because they conceive of themselves by means of names, thinking ‘I am this,’ they then disparage other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”

Because of this negligence, they depart from the omniscience of the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha and distance themselves from *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means). Thus, they consider themselves to have departed from the *prajñāpāramitā*, to have departed from the good teacher, and to have obtained an evil teacher. Such bodhisattvas will inevitably fall into one of two paths: the stage of the śrāvaka or the pratyekabuddha path.

If one seeks Buddhahood again after enduring great hardship for a very long time, by virtue of the grace of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one shall once more attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and personally achieve the state of an *arhat* (A-vi-san-fo).
The Buddha said:

"At that time, when one forms this intention and receives these names, if one does not immediately awaken to it and repent, such a person shall fall into the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha paths."
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus, there are four grave prohibitions; if one commits any other offense among them, one no longer becomes a śramaṇa and is no longer a son of the Buddha."
The sin of destroying such a bodhisattva is heavier than the four grave prohibitions for a bhikṣu.
This bodhisattva says:
"My name is so-and-so; I was born in such-and-such a country."
He thought to himself: "This transgression is more grave than the four pārājika offenses and even exceeds the five heinous crimes.
Why is the offense so grave?
It is because, for the sake of receiving the name, he does not recognize the subtle workings of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
regarding the virtue of seclusion:
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing it, Māra the Evil One may appear before them and speak as follows:"
"The Dharma of seclusion is precisely thus, as praised by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"I do not speak of such seclusion when I instruct bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to dwell alone in solitary places, among trees, or in quiet retreats."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha:
“How is it, O God among Gods!
Is there a distinct form of seclusion for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the indistinct, this is the contemplation of a śrāvaka.
To contemplate the indistinct is the contemplation of a pratyekabuddha."
The one who practices in the state of vagueness is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; although dwelling in cities and towns, they continue to practice seclusion.
The one who practices in the state of vagueness is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, for whom no unwholesome dharmas arise.

One who practices in a state of transcendental detachment is a bodhisattva mahāsattva; if they dwell alone among the trees or in a secluded place, this bodhisattva mahāsattva continues to practice seclusion.

This is what I delight in having the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice; this is the practice of seclusion, which should be kept in mind day and night. This is the practice of seclusion for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, the practice of seclusion for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices seclusion, even while remaining near a city, he continues to practice in a state of profound detachment; likewise, whether he dwells alone among the trees in a secluded place, he remains in a state of profound detachment, and while dwelling alone among the trees in a secluded place, he practices in a state of profound detachment.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva thinks to himself,
"I have realized seclusion.
At that time, Māra the Evil One approaches and instructs him to practice seclusion, saying:
"If one dwells in solitude, among the trees, or in a quiet place, one should practice in this manner.
Thus, following the instructions of Māra, that bodhisattva loses the state of seclusion.
Māra spoke again:
"The Way is entirely equal; the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are all conceived in this same way without distinction.
Those who conceive it thus are those who fulfill the prajñāpāramitā, and they should practice in this manner."
The Buddha said:

"The dharmas contemplated by this bodhisattva-mahāsattva are not pure; that is to say, because he follows [such practices], he instead uses them to look down upon other bodhisattvas, thinking to himself:
'Who could surpass me!'"

He treats with contempt those bodhisattvas who practice purity near the city—those whose thoughts do not enter the teachings of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, who harbor no evil intentions, and who do not receive the joy of dhyāna, samādhi, or samāpatti; yet they have all attained their aspirations and are fully endowed with the means of deliverance.
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva who lacks *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), even if they were to dwell in a wilderness four thousand li wide where neither birds nor beasts go, nor thieves, nor rākṣasas can reach;..."

Even if they remain there for one year, a hundred years, a thousand years, a hundred thousand years, a hundred million years, or a hundred billion years—even if it exceeds these durations—if they do not know how to practice detachment, it will ultimately be of no benefit, and they will be unable to fulfill the detachment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
He thought to himself:
"I have fully attained it;
I have fully realized it."
Then Māra went and flew into the air, saying these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"

This is true detachment, as taught by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; one should practice this very detachment, for in doing so, one will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the supreme perfect enlightenment.

Upon hearing this, that bodhisattva-mahāsattva rises from his seclusion and departs, going instead to where other bodhisattvas who practice seclusion near a city reside, or to where bhikṣus who have accomplished the path of a practitioner dwell; there, being full of self-conceit, he conversely goes to disparage them, saying:
"The Dharma you practice is actually not the Dharma."
The Buddha said:
"Those who follow the practice of vagueness and confusion are correct, yet they are called wrong;
those among them who act contrarily are called correct."
To show respect to those who do not deserve it, while instead feeling anger toward those who truly deserve respect—
this is what is meant by saying, "My conduct is far removed from the truth."
For this reason, non-human beings came to me and said:
"Excellent, excellent!
What you practice is truly such a state of seclusion."
"If you were to dwell near a city, who would come to speak to you?
Who would inform you?
The Buddha said:
"This Bodhisattva is a person of virtue, yet they instead despise him.
Thus, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva should know that such a person is like one who carries a corpse; they are no longer fit for anything."

To instead call out the faults of a bodhisattva is to act as an enemy to that bodhisattva. One who seeks to disparage a bodhisattva is a great thief in this world and the world beyond; even if they wear the robes of a śramaṇa, they are still a thief, and they are likewise a thief among those bodhisattvas who possess virtuous qualities.
Subhūti, one should not engage in affairs with such persons;
one should not converse with them; nor should one regard them with respect.
Why is this? You should know that such persons frequently give rise to anger and destroy the good intentions of others.
What do you think, Subhūti?
Does this bodhisattva-mahāsattva not relinquish sarvajñā (all-knowledge) nor abandon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not relinquish sarvajñā, it is for this reason that he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and becomes a refuge for all people.
These bodhisattvas should not associate with those who ruin others nor should they show them respect.
They should not congregate with such people, but rather should protect the Dharma.

They should maintain it firmly and keep it in mind; they should always stand in awe of the realm of birth and death and its places of toil and suffering, and should never enter therein, remaining uninvolved with the three realms.
Wherever those bodhisattvas who have fallen away reside, you should always protect them with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion.
You should reflect:
"May I never give rise to such evil thoughts as to cause them harm."
"If there should be anything unwholesome, may I quickly abandon it;
this is because I must practice learning.
This, Subhūti, is [the way].
This is the supreme knowledge of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Chapter Twelve: On Good Spiritual Friends.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and become perfectly awakened ones (tathāgatas) should draw near to good spiritual friends, engage in their service, and honor them with devoted attendance."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O God among Gods! Who are the good spiritual friends of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
"How should one know this?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is the good spiritual friend of the bodhisattva mahāsattva."

Regarding those who speak of the Prajñāpāramitā: if, from what they have heard of the Prajñāpāramitā, they themselves cross over and teach others how to enter into it and practice accordingly, know that such persons are the good spiritual teachers of these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The six pāramitās are the good teachers of the bodhisattva;
the six pāramitās are the sūtra; the six pāramitās are the path; the six pāramitās serve to dispel darkness; the six pāramitās are themselves the platform; the six pāramitās are themselves the light.

Because all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past emerged from the six pāramitās; all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas yet to come in the future will emerge from the six pāramitās; and all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently existing in incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands have emerged from the six pāramitās and attained sarvajñatā—all of them did so by bestowing upon others four kinds of gifts:
first, material giving; second, joy; third, benefit; and fourth, impartiality.
Subhūti, this is the śāstra of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva;

it is their mother, it is their father, it is their home, it is their platform, it is their protection, it is their refuge, and it is their guide. These are all the six pāramitās, and they are that which benefits all people.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the six pāramitās, because they employ the ultimate absence of [inherent existence], they desire to sever the doubts of others; for this reason, they should study the prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha:
"O World-Honored One! What is the characteristic of the prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“The characteristic of the Prajñāpāramitā is that it is without obstruction. Subhūti said:
“As the God among Gods has taught, these characteristics are indeed the *prajñāpāramitā*.
One who possesses such characteristics attains all dharmas.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Subhūti!
That which is the mark of suchness (tathatā-lakṣaṇa) attains the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); that which has such a mark attains all dharmas."
Why is this? Subhūti, all dharmas are but fleeting illusions; all dharmas are empty.
For this reason, Subhūti,
that which is illusory and empty is the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The characteristics of all dharmas are also illusory, and this emptiness is likewise illusory.
Subhūti! The Tathāgata has taught that all dharmas are entirely evanescent and empty. Why is this so?
Human desire for existence has no end; that which is ethereal is without desire, and that which is ethereal is without birth.
That which is empty is without desire, and that which is empty is without anything born.
The *ānantarya-samādhi* and emptiness are not the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained from a dharma other than the *ānantarya-samādhi* and emptiness.
"How, O Tathāgata, can that which you have spoken be understood?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"People have been thinking and speaking thus for a long time:"
"It is mine, it is not mine. It is for this reason, and by means of this, that one arrives at such a state. Subhūti said:
"So it is, O God among Gods!
Regarding the person spoken of, he has indeed long since thought and said: 'This is mine; this is not mine.'"
The Buddha said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Is that which belongs to me empty?"
Subhūti said: "This is emptiness,
O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Is that which does not belong to me empty?"
Subhūti said: "This is emptiness,
O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Because of this, people think to themselves: 'This is mine; this is not mine.'"
"Because of this, one remains within birth and death without end.
Subhūti said, "It is so."
"O God among Gods!
Because of this, people remain in birth and death without any time of rest.
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti, it should be understood that this person,
following their desires, becomes attached among persons."
One should not have anything to seek; subsequently, one will no longer be attached to that truth. Subhūti!
When there is something added, one should not think:
"This is mine; this is not mine"—to practice in this way is to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), Subhūti. This is it, Subhūti!
"That which is produced does not subsequently undergo such production; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"O God among Gods, one who practices in this manner..."
It is because one does not practice with regard to form, nor does one practice with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. O God among Gods!
That which is thus practiced is what the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates as conforming to worldly convention; this is the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
O God among Gods!
This is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and is the sphere of practice for all people.
It is the ultimate of the past; because there is no one who can attain that which has been attained therein, this constitutes the supreme excellence of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
O God among Gods!
That which is thus contemplated is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner day and night, according to such practice, he will swiftly approach the seat of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?

Suppose all the people of Jambudvīpa, as well as all bodhisattvas, were made into human beings, and they all practiced *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, having resolved their minds to seek Buddhahood; each of them, throughout the span of their lives, performed acts of giving, and taking these gifts, they offered them for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the merit of this bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices such giving not great?
Subhūti replied, "Very great, very great!"
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"It is not as meritorious as the practice of a single day by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who focuses single-mindedly on the prajñāpāramitā; its merit surpasses the former."
Or, if there is a bodhisattva who is single-mindedly mindful of the Prajñāpāramitā and acts in accordance with it, such a person is the most supreme and honored among the assembly. Why is this?
Other people do not possess such loving-kindness; with the exception of the Buddhas, there is no one equal to this Mahāsattva.
The realm entered by this son of good family is exceedingly profound; he understands, fully knows, and perceives the world—this is itself great compassion.
His eye sees through to the far reaches, perceiving incalculable beings; he desires to see them all without a moment of weariness.
He contemplates all people without forming conceptualizations, nor does he perceive any distinction between them.
