Subhūti, this is the great illumination of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Although they have not yet attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi as an arhat-buddha, this is precisely what they practice.
That practice is most sublime, transcending the world, and from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* one shall never again regress.

One who receives clothing, food, bedding, and medicine from others, while their mind abides in the *prajñāpāramitā*, remains pure in virtue despite receiving such gifts; the merit they produce brings them close to the seat of *sarvajñatā*.
Therefore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva eats, there is no fault, for he desires to benefit all people and intends to show them the path.

To possess illumination and a profound desire to cross over the great and limitless [samsara], to wish for the complete liberation of all those within the prisons [of existence], and to desire that the eyes of all people become entirely pure—this is what is intended by the Prajñāpāramitā.
One who practices in accordance with this teaching and maintains mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā* is thereby unshakable.
Why is this? That which causes movement involves conceptualization; such is not the *prajñāpāramitā*, and it is not protection.
One should practice in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā* and keep it in mind day and night.
Subhūti, it is like a man who, having previously not obtained a *maṇi* jewel, later obtains one; he is filled with joy and leaps for gladness.
Having obtained a maṇi jewel, he then lost it.
Because of this loss, he became greatly afflicted with grief;
whether sitting or rising, he was filled with sorrow and found no relief.
In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who seeks the precious jewel should always firmly maintain the mind and never lose the mindfulness of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha:
“All mental engagements are by nature detached from intrinsic being.
How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva engages with sarvajñā (all-knowledge) without being detached from such engagement?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has such knowledge as this, they do not lose the prajñāpāramitā. Why is that?
"Subhūti! This Prajñāpāramitā is emptiness; it neither increases nor decreases. Subhūti said:
“O Devātideva! Since the Prajñāpāramitā is truly emptiness,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva increase in the Prajñāpāramitā, perfect their practice, and draw near to the seat of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva neither increases nor decreases.
When this Dharma is being taught, those who hear it are not terrified and not afraid.”
"You should know that this son of good family is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti said to the Buddha,
"Is the perfection of wisdom a practice of emptiness?"
He replied, "No, Subhūti."
“Is it possible to practice the perfection of wisdom while being distinct from emptiness? He replied, “No.”
"Subhūti! Is this the practice of form?
He replied:
"No, Subhūti! Is it for the sake of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?"
He replied: "No, Subhūti."
“Can there be a different color as its objective sphere? He replied, “No.”
"Subhūti! Can there be any other formations of feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness?
He replied:
"No, Subhūti! How so, O God among Gods?"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said,
“What do you think, Subhūti?”
"Is it for the sake of seeing dharmas, or for the sake of the practice of dharmas, that one practices the Prajñāpāramitā?
Subhūti replied, "No,
I do not see them."
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
“Can a bodhisattva mahāsattva see themselves practicing the prajñāpāramitā?
Subhūti replied, “No, he cannot.”
“O God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
“What do you think, Subhūti?”
“Can one see any place where dharmas arise? Subhūti replied, “No.”
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patient acceptance of the non-arising of all phenomena."

One who is thus has received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is the fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices these deeds and possesses this power, they shall attain the Buddha-wisdom; this is indeed Great Wisdom.
"Furthermore, the wisdom of mastery, the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and the wisdom of the Tathāgata—if these do not exist, one cannot be capable of this state oneself.
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"Do all dharmas receive the prediction for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from that which is unproduced?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti, “No.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha:
"How is it, O God among Gods!
How does one bestow the prediction upon a bodhisattva mahāsattva so that they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"One who is able to see the Dharma for oneself receives the prediction of attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti said:
"I do not see any dharma that shall become Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"All dharmas are unattainable.
One who forms this thought will achieve the state of an Arhat-samyak-saṃbuddha."
"If one does not act in this way, one will not personally attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. 13.
The Chapter on Śakra Devānām Indra. Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha from within the assembly, saying:
"Profound, indeed profound is the *prajñāpāramitā*, O God among Gods!"
It is difficult to comprehend;
the deeds of a bodhisattva are elusive.
If there are virtuous people who, upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, write it down, uphold it, and study it, their merit will not be small.
The Buddha said to Kauśika:

"If all the people of Jambudvīpa were to practice the ten wholesome deeds, their merit would be a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-millionfold, or even a billionfold—and more than that—yet it would still not equal that of a son or daughter of good family who hears, writes down, upholds, and studies the Prajñāpāramitā."
Among those seated, there was a bhikṣu who said to Śakra Devānām Indra,
"This surpasses you, O Kauśika.
Śakra Devānām Indra replied to that bhikṣu:

"One who turns their mind for even a single moment of reflection surpasses me; how much more so those who hear the Prajñāpāramitā, write it down, uphold it, and study it, and who, having heard it, establish themselves according to these teachings—they altogether surpass all devas, asuras, and worldly humans."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not merely surpass the devas, asuras, and worldly humans; they surpass all of them, including the srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they not only surpass the pratyekabuddhas, but also transcend those bodhisattvas who practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) without skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and are thus devoid of the perfection [of wisdom].

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not merely transcend the perfection of giving; they likewise practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditation, yet they do so without skillful means and apart from the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva further recites and practices the Prajñāpāramitā, then even all the devas, asuras, and people of the world combined could never surpass that bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the Prajñāpāramitā; this is because they regard it as supreme and remain close to the Prajñāpāramitā.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva follows sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), and thus it is said that there is nothing to be severed.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from the name of the tathāgata; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s attainment of non-separation from the Buddha’s seat.

All laziness that this bodhisattva-mahāsattva possesses no longer arises; the training of this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is the training in the supreme, for he does not train in the training of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—this training is the training of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
The Four Heavenly Kings shall go to inquire after his well-being, so that he may joyfully and swiftly attain this training.
He shall sit upon the seat of the Buddha, personally realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and deliver the fourfold assembly of disciples.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, the Four Heavenly Kings shall go to inquire after his welfare, let alone other devaputras.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the prajñāpāramitā is constantly held in the thoughts of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

The perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is the practice of a bodhisattva; if there are any afflictions of toil and suffering in the world, this body shall never experience such evils. This is brought about by the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, whereby one immediately attains the merit of the present dharma.
Ānanda had this thought:
"Does Śakra Devānām Indra speak this by his own wisdom,
or does he speak it through the Buddha’s majestic power?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing what Ānanda was thinking in his mind, immediately said to Ānanda:
"What I have spoken was sustained by the Buddha's majestic spiritual power.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Ānanda!
All that Śakra Devānām-indra has spoken is brought about by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha."
At times, Ānanda,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva deeply contemplates the practice of the prajñāpāramitā, they then contemplate and train in the prajñāpāramitā.

At that time, all the wicked Māras within the trichiliocosm were filled with grief and distress, desiring to cause the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva to realize the limit of reality midway through his path, thereby leading him to attain the way of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha.
"If they cause [beings] to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they will swiftly achieve A-vy-ava-buddha-hood.
